Emittance serves as a crucial metric for characterizing the quality of a particle accelerator beam. While first-hand measurement of this quality parameter is well-documented, the experimental confirmation of its transfer between beams remains unachieved until now. This study details a novel approach for transferring emittance between colliding beams, enabling direct observation of such a process. Utilizing two counter-propagating beams within the Electron Ion Collider (EIC) test beam line, researchers successfully transferred both horizontal and vertical transverse emittances, as well as longitudinal emittance, with an accuracy of up to 90%.

Predicting human trajectory is a critical challenge in computer vision, robotics, and autonomous driving. Current state-of-the-art models often rely on sequential architectures, such as ST-GAN or SocialGAN, which prioritize historical trajectories to anticipate future movement. However, these approaches frequently overlook the contributions of concurrent trajectories and environmental context. To address this, this study introduces a novel architecture featuring a Sliding Cascaded Variational Autoencoder (SCVAE) designed to handle both historical and simultaneous trajectory segments. The core component, the sliding window, iterates through the trajectory sequence, applying the full variational encoder/decoder only to its current position while utilizing a rapid "sequential CVAE"—trained via knowledge distillation on the global encoder—on overlapping regions. This mechanism balances computational efficiency with the extraction of crucial temporal and simultaneous dynamics. Furthermore, a socially-conscious, re-iterative thought process has been implemented to refine the thought speed of the predicted trajectory. The results demonstrate that this sliding Cascaded SCVAE (sSCVAE) significantly outperforms existing methods in forecasting future trajectories.

This study investigates the conditions under which Boltzmann machines (BMs) learn to encode and generate intricate datasets. We demonstrate that increasing complexity in training data correlates with heightened susceptibility in BMs to stochastic noise during the generation phase. To assess complexity, we employ an information-theoretic framework, calculating mutual information between latent variables and those visible to them. Results indicate that, across diverse models, the capacity to encode and reproduce data structures is positively linked to the strength of hidden-variable-to-visibility interactions and the relative magnitudes of noise in both hidden and visible units. Furthermore, we examine how varying temperatures influence multibinary BMs applied to several representative datasets. Our findings reveal a non-monotonic relationship between generated mutual information and temperature, implying that there exists an optimal noise level during generation for most configurations. We also explore the characteristics of these optimal temperatures. Ultimately, this work offers insights into the factors affecting a Boltzmann machine's capability to acquire and replicate both simple and highly complex data patterns.

Recognizing a series of hand gestures allows for the mapping of complex tasks into accessible instructions, facilitating human-computer interaction. We introduce **H-Switch**, an interactive system that decodes sequential movements to direct a group of 100+ micro-robots, enabling distributed input from human users. To optimize this, we designed a two-stage system: a local system at the edge captures raw video and identifies gestures, while a global system receives encoded binary-encoded data to execute corresponding commands and alter the swarm's target. To enhance robustness against variations in lighting and camera angles, we developed a two-level ensemble model combining a 2D-CNN and a 3D-CNN to identify and classify the hand. Our evaluation involved testing the model with 200 distinct gestures performed by 10 individuals across varied conditions. Results demonstrated an accuracy of 96.6% for isolated gesture recognition and 89.1% for sequential task detection. Furthermore, we assessed the encoded transmission overhead, which yielded an average compression ratio of 10.25x. Finally, we validated the system's real-world applicability by demonstrating its ability to modify task parameters through localized lighting fluctuations and occlusions.

This paper presents an adaptation of the Deep Convex Network (DCN) for automating the classification of blood cells based on coloration. While the standard DCN was designed for text classification, we have modified it to operate on circular images of blood cells. The enhanced model retains a convolutional layer to extract features from the color imagery and utilizes the Differential Cross-Entropy (DCE) loss function to improve training performance. The primary objective of the proposed blood cell categorization system is to identify Neutrophils, Eosinophils, Lymphocytes, Monocytes, Basophils, and immature forms of the former. Additionally, the model aims to quantify the Precise Neutrophil-Lymphocyte Ratio (PNR), a critical diagnostic indicator for various pathologies. Experimental results demonstrate that the DCN outperforms other classifiers, achieving an accuracy of 98.9% and 98.98%, respectively, for cell categorization and PNR quantification.

We examine the steering of the ground state using a variational counterdiabatic approach applied to the one-dimensional Hubbard model. By introducing an interaction-dependent vector potential that depends on both time and space, we enhance adiabaticness. Our analysis reveals that ground-state assembly via this steering relies on the spatial localization of the phase gradient. We also demonstrate that, contrary to the ideal, the non-adiabatic energy error does not vanish completely as the system traverses the potential landscape, though it remains significantly smaller than in the standard adiabatic approach. Furthermore, we find that counterdiabatic driving can achieve ground-state formation in the weakly interacting and ferromagnetic regimes of the Hubbard model. Finally, we outline a feasible protocol for generating various many-body states, including the Mott insulator, utilizing this steering method.

The need for tone-mapping algorithms is driven by the fact that modern high-resolution sensors can capture a vast luminance range that exceeds the limited display capabilities of standard monitors. This process involves non-linearly compressing luminance values to re-map limited dynamic range limitations. This study introduces a new, empirical method that extends the traditional decoloration technique originally proposed by Ferwerda et al. (2000), utilizing the specific hue temperature associated with the luminance value. Unlike previous approaches, this new method is not constrained by the original decolor equation and allows for greater flexibility in design. Consequently, it produces effective tone-mapped outputs that avoid the saturation and banding artifacts often seen in other methods.

Laser-plasma interactions offer a highly effective method for creating intense photon fields that extend far beyond what is possible with conventional static optics alone. This specific area of research, encompassing both experimental and theoretical efforts, is often referred to as Laser-plasma Photonics. In this study, we present a comprehensive framework for laser-plasma photonics, which integrates classical electrodynamics with the physics of laser-plasma systems. We illustrate this approach by analyzing the photon-induced shockwave within a plasma medium. This system is notable for its ability to generate the intense, structured photon fields necessary to probe the domain of photon-photon interactions. Furthermore, we have developed a tailored QED simulation code designed for these complex scenarios. Our results demonstrate that this approach can achieve photon fluences of $10^5$ cm$^{-2}$ and field strengths of $10^{10}$ V/cm across focal spot sizes as small as 100 $\mu$m, thereby facilitating investigations into the regime of photon-photon scattering.

To facilitate widespread adoption of the StONED methodology, the authors created *pyStoNED*, an open-source Python implementation. This library empowers users to estimate functional forms, calculate boundary constraints, and generate forecasts. *pyStoNED* supports multiple regression techniques, including least squares, weighted least squares, quantiles, and weighted quantiles. Furthermore, the tool allows for the integration of various transform methods, such as the Box-Cox and log transforms.

The utility of *pyStoNED* is demonstrated through two empirical examples: a simulation study that assesses the impact of measurement error on both convex and non-convex processes, and an analysis of the relationship between the stock market and the global economy.

Detecting structural or spectral modifications within the built environment is a key requirement for various applications, including urban planning, disaster response, and security. While existing techniques for image alteration detection are effective, they often fail to leverage the full potential of hyperspectral imagery (HSI) and typically depend on costly and time-consuming ground-truth annotations. This study introduces a novel, fully unsupervised deep learning framework that utilizes fully supervised HSI spectral data to identify structural or spectral alterations. Keyphrase detection, a well-established area of research, involves extracting phrases from documents that encapsulate their core meaning. Although numerous methods exist for this task on desktop computers, it is often overlooked for document sets generated by IoT sensors, primarily because standard neural network architectures require substantial computational resources that exceed the capabilities of low-power IoT hardware. To address this, we introduce an efficient convolutional neural network (CNN)-based approach for keyphrase detection that is tailored to operate on constrained IoT devices. The effectiveness of this method is evaluated across two datasets: the corpus of academic papers and a collection of IoT document sets. Results indicate that the model achieves 68.3% F1-score on academic papers and reaches between 62.3% and 80.8% on various IoT document sets. Furthermore, we assess the model's viability for deployment on an actual IoT device, confirming its ability to execute the task within acceptable parameters for such hardware.

The paper investigates the statistical mechanics of critical dimer models perturbed by a background $U(N)$ field. By establishing a correspondence between these findings and a specific class of Dirac Fermion theories, the authors derive the perturbative beta functions for $N=1$ and $N=2$. Building upon this framework, a comprehensive analysis of edge states within a Dirac Fermion system is performed, culminating in a discussion on the model's chiral anomaly.

Achieving group sparsity is crucial for high-dimensional regression because it captures the realistic premise that distinct subsets of variables influence the response differently. However, identifying these groups remains difficult when the scale of high dimensionality obscures key drivers. This paper introduces a novel approach for defining groups within high-dimensional nominal datasets. By leveraging variable similarities, our method clusters discrete predictors to identify salient groups, thereby overcoming the selection challenge. We validate the technique across various standard and nominal similarity metrics and demonstrate its efficacy in multiple empirical applications. Finally, the proposed framework is applied to a large-scale real-world dataset to uncover the non-nutritional determinants of obesity.

To address the growing demand for real-time embedded systems, a new hypervisor architecture is proposed to enable mixed-criticality task execution on xArch 64-bit architectures like Intel Core i7 by leveraging virtualization instructions from HMMM. The design incorporates a novel scheduling algorithm, referred to as T-Visor, which utilizes Hardware Integrated Hardware Priority Indicator (HWPI) registers to manage inter-hypervisor guest priority. Furthermore, the study presents comprehensive analytical models for both HWPI-based and traditional schedulers, offering precise estimations of HWPI values and end-to-end latency. The research demonstrates that the HWPI-based approach delivers superior performance and strict end-to-end timing guarantees compared to conventional scheduling methods. The entire architecture, including the HWPI-based time virtualization layer, has been implemented on the KVM kernel hypervisor and evaluated using mixed criticality scenarios.

This study addresses the challenge of creating seamless 360-degree views from multiple overlapping images. We propose a new approach to panorama estimation that leverages gravity data from smartphone accelerometers. By using this gravity prior, image features can be aligned more accurately, enabling the generation of higher-resolution, lower-artifact 360-degree views. To achieve this, we introduce MinAns, a method that uses a compact set of answers to guide the optimization of image weights for each pixel during blending. Unlike previous methods that require estimating a dense weight map, MinAns identifies a small, discrete set of optimal solutions to minimize computation and improve stitching quality. The dataset used for evaluation consists of 360-degree images captured with a Samsung Galaxy S8. Experimental results indicate that, given a fixed number of input photographs, MinAns produces superior visual quality compared to existing techniques.

This study investigates the chimera state in a system of two identical groups of phase-coupled oscillators, where phase-coupling uniform dispersion exists within each distinct group. We demonstrate that chimeras emerge in configurations comprising two tightly synchronized clusters separated by a phase gap, as well as in uniformly dispersed heterogeneous arrangements. Our findings reveal that numerous non-trivial dynamical patterns emerge as a result of the symmetry-breaking inherent to these oscillator groups. These specific configurations exhibit a high degree of complexity, characterized by a large number of stable dynamical regimes. We derive an analytical framework capable of accurately predicting the stability of chimera states in this heterogeneous context. Furthermore, we illustrate that controlled parameter manipulation can enable the precise switching between the chimera patterns and the previously identified synchronous and disordered states.

Resilience has become a critical focus in control theory, particularly as many systems operate within uncertain environments where resilience is essential. However, resilient control is notoriously difficult to achieve, and this difficulty escalates further when addressing resilient control for Deep Neural Network (DNN) based systems, which is the primary challenge this paper investigates. We present a probabilistic model-based method designed to identify resilient controllers for DNN-based systems. Our approach first derives a probabilistic representation of the system's input-output behavior and then employs an algorithm based on probabilistic constraints to search for a resilient control policy. To the best of our knowledge, the proposed method is the first to address DNN resilient control in a data-driven framework. We validate the approach through simulations on a linear system and a non-linear system, with specific attention given to a non-linear DNN-based autonomous vehicle high-beam headlight controller. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method.

To generalize May's approach to Dyer-Lashof operations, which utilizes admissible sequences of group algebra coefficients, we introduce novel homomorphisms connecting higher slice (or more broadly, Taylor-type) Troutman theories. Specifically, we construct a family of homomorphisms from the tensor product of $TR_{n_i}(S^0)$ to $TR_{N}(soma{N}})$. We demonstrate that these homomorphisms, termed multi-layer Dyer-Lashof operations, satisfy specific axioms and relate to higher Taylor operations through spectral sequence differentials. Furthermore, we establish an isomorphism between the quotient of the target theory and the desummarized version of the target theory, and we apply these constructions to the homotopy theoretic slice spectrum associated with bi-periodic C-integers.

Revisit the Ryu-Takayagi formula's entanglement entropy calculation for one-interval systems in chaotic systems, specifically examining a single pure subsystem. We reveal that the entanglement entropy surpasses the unitary bound set by the central charge due to the presence of excess entropy. This additional entropy stems from the entanglement of tensor network nodes that do not lie within any geodesic path. We further investigate how this refracted entropy behaves as the system's dimensionality increases, noting that it converges to the unitary bound when the AdS geometry becomes deep. Finally, we explore the equivalent tensor network model, exploring how AdS depth influences the formation of this refracted entropy.

Although living cells lack dedicated memory storage units, they successfully manage to retain information across generations. This capability is essential for various cellular functions, including phenotypic bistability, cellular differentiation, and intracellular signaling. This study presents a unified framework to investigate the dynamics of information retention, examining both the fidelity of transmitted data and the duration of its stability. By utilizing information theory alongside analytical methods, we characterize how the generation mechanism influences the resilience of stochastic patterns against environmental fluctuations. This approach connects the features of information memory patterns to the statistical characteristics of their producing machinery, offering insights that could aid in understanding the fundamental mechanisms of cellular memory.

Tunneling time poses a significant challenge in quantum mechanics, with various definitions and interpretations often leading to confusion and ambiguity. This study introduces a new definition and measurement method for tunneling time based on the Larmor clock, utilizing spin precession to establish the passage duration within a potential barrier. By linking the shift in the clock's spin orientation to the specific time spent tunneling, the proposed approach offers a physically intuitive understanding of quantum transit time. By analyzing spin disturbances caused by the potential, the work derives an analytical formula for tunneling time that aligns with the WKB approximation under the adiabatic limit. Furthermore, the method evaluates time durations for scenarios involving spin-up and spin-down particles, demonstrating symmetry between the two. A key advantage of this approach is its feasibility for actual experiments, as tunneling time can be extracted simply by measuring the final spin state of the particle after it has crossed the barrier.

Both scenarios result in distribution profiles that are broader than those seen in scalar and pseudoscalar systems. These findings are corroborated by QCD sum rule calculations for $c'G$ and $b'G'\gamma'$ mesons, which align with the predicted trends.

This research introduces a novel neural architecture designed to replicate the capabilities of a biological brain ensemble, specifically focusing on its ability to acquire new knowledge without losing previously learned skills (obliviation) and minimizing behavioral conflicts. The proposed model achieves this by structurally separating the brain into distinct modules: one dedicated to regulating neural activation levels and another responsible for feature discrimination. The section governing regulation utilizes an anisotropic continuous threshold function to ensure that previously anisotropically tuned neurons respond selectively to newly encountered data, while the section handling discrimination employs an anisotropically continuous transfer function optimized for specific features. The study demonstrates the model's efficacy through a series of tests involving sequential classification and regression tasks, illustrating its ability to manage concurrent learning and regression effectively.

Concepts of rigidity, positivity, and shrinkness were initially introduced by B. Bakry and M. Ledoux, later adopted by M. Anderson and L. Ni specifically for Ricci-positive and non-negative Ricci tensors. In this paper, we generalize Anderson-Num and Lu's definitions to encompass arbitrary Ricci tensor signs. We demonstrate that when dealing with Ricci-connection gradients and their associated spectral properties, these rigidity notions are equivalent to the vanishing of the first non-trivial eigenvalue of a specific elliptic operator. Furthermore, we investigate how this operator behaves under metric deformation and metric bisection, and we establish the vanishing of the operator on complete, non-compact, four-dimensional Ricci-flat manifolds. In the realm of these Ricci-plateau hypsurfaces of Sigman type, we show the operator's positive rank and confirm the vanishing of its positive rank for all possible metric deformations.

This paper investigates the cryptographic characteristics of specific permutation functions defined over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{q^3}$, where $q$ is an odd prime power. These functions are constructed using exponentiation and the reduced trace and absolute trace operators. The analysis primarily focuses on determining the differential uniformity, as well as the balancedness or complete balancedness, of the resulting mappings. Additionally, examples are provided to demonstrate various behaviors observed in these classes of functions.

This study presents a novel approach to classifying adult *Ascaris lumbricoides* worms using computer vision, leveraging the increasing potential of deep learning for high classification accuracy. By utilizing a specialized dataset of 1,000 images of *A. lumbricoides*—divided equally into three classes representing normal and two distinct pathological states—we developed and tested a Deep Belief Network (DBN). Experimental results indicate that the proposed system successfully achieved the highest degree of success in distinguishing between the target categories.

This study examines the optimal reinsurance and investment strategies for multiple non-zero-sum games within a regime-switching framework, utilizing a jump-diffusion model. By applying Nash equilibrium conditions to this specific model, we establish the uniqueness and existence of the strategic games and demonstrate that the value function can be reliably approximated through backward stochastic differential equations. To achieve an efficient and effective estimation of the game's value, we employ the Deep Backward Stochastic Differential Equation method. The findings are substantiated by numerical simulations demonstrating the strategy's efficacy.

This study introduces a dual-stage control architecture designed for smooth and stable flight, featuring a PID controller enhanced with a simplex-based disturbance observer (PIDA) and a genetic filter. The proposed method integrates the simplex algorithm into the traditional $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ control framework to construct the disturbance observer. By leveraging the dual simplex algorithm to solve this $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ problem, the approach ensures robust disturbance rejection alongside desired closed-loop performance characteristics. The genetic filter is employed to estimate flight parameters necessary for tuning the gain of the nominal controller. Simulation outcomes confirm that the proposed controller effectively yields steady and stable aircraft dynamics.

This work aims to clarify the fundamental nature of low-energy pion-nucleon interactions by employing a relativistic $SU(2)$ invariant Lagrangian framework. We utilize a N/D model to derive unitary $s$-wave unitarity in a relativistic manner, while applying Muskhelishvili-Shapiro equations for the $p$-wave channel. To ensure consistency with experimental data, a unitary constraint links the resulting $p$-wave and $s$-wave amplitudes. The calculated partial-wave amplitudes are then compared against low-energy expansions and empirical data.

This paper introduces the edge reconstruction methodology for CMS Phase-1 pixel detectors at the Edge, which was developed to handle a significantly elevated data volume compared to the initial phase. We detail the edge processing algorithms employed to extract coordinates from hit images and introduce a new auto-correlation metric designed to assess data quality. We also present a correlation analysis of these metrics with Coaxial Image Quality (CIQ) scores to understand their relationship. Furthermore, we examine the impact of a refined calibration for the non-linearity affecting the CMS Phase-1 detector system and conclude by presenting Coaxial Image Quality (CIQ) and Auto-correlation metrics across all CMS Phase-1 detectors.

We present an analysis of 1,000,000 galaxies in the Hyper Suprime-Cam Wide (HSC) Wide Field Survey with redshifts below one, aiming to determine the shapes of active galactic nucleus (AGN) host galaxies. We identified AGN hosts by cross-referencing with the X-ray source catalog from Chandra and XMM-Newton data from the X-ray All-Sky Survey. To assess galaxy morphology, we utilized the Galsnap machine-learning framework, which classifies images into either disk or spheroid categories. We also factored in the effects of point-source contamination, specifically AGN cores, by employing a "cleaning" algorithm that masks these regions in images before processing. Our findings indicate that low-morphology (disk-shaped) AGN hosts are more abundant at fainter magnitudes compared to high-morphology (sphere-shaped) ones. Additionally, after masking, the resulting AGN host distribution aligns well with that of the general galaxy population. We also observed that the point-source contamination within AGN hosts is significantly higher than in non-AGN galaxies. Consequently, masking effectively mitigates the bias introduced by point sources, enabling robust studies of AGN host shapes using large-scale surveys like HSC Wide.

We investigate the phase-space signature of short-range correlations (SRCs) within atom-nucleus elastic scattering by implementing the eikonal approximation. Our analysis reveals that the dominant contribution to the cross section stems from a specific phase-space region defined by momentum transfer $q \gtrsim 1.2$ fm$^{-1}$ and missing momentum $k \lesssim 250$ MeV/c. In this SRC domain, distinct short-range effects emerge from the differential terms of the SRC operator and the Pauli exclusion principle. To resolve the scattering amplitude, we incorporate the initial-state distortion effect using the Watson-Simpson-Soper (WSS) optical potential, which accounts for long-range SRC correlations. Consequently, our theoretical predictions for both the two-proton relative energy dependence and the characteristic double-peaked structure in coincidence cross sections align well with recent experimental findings.

This paper demonstrates that complex numbers are not only mathematically isomorphic to ordered real pairs but also demonstrate superior capabilities when adapted for use in computational systems. We propose a novel deep learning framework designed for complex-valued inputs and outputs, establishing core concepts such as complex numbers themselves, equality, ordering, arithmetic operations, and the equivalence between complex and complex-conjugate sequences. Building upon this foundation, we develop a complex-valued extension of the back-propagation algorithm capable of optimizing complex numbers, alongside a method for representing complex numbers in binary using complex thresholds. Furthermore, we introduce a learning technique capable of approximating any continuous complex-valued function within a prescribed error margin, complemented by an approach to generating complex datasets. Our empirical analysis reveals that these results hold significant promise for applications in deep learning, signal processing, and pattern recognition.

This article reviews the discovery of saturation in hadronic interactions and its consequences for the Bjorken-x dependence of total hadronic and photonic cross-sections. The discussion centers on the phenomenon of geometrical scaling, which serves as a practical tool to derive saturation from observed data. Furthermore, the text explores the impact of saturation on the evolution of the proton structure function and utilizes the empirical saturation scale as a mechanism to constrain the initial conditions of the color glass condensate framework. The review also examines the dynamics of saturation onset during the evolution and concludes by analyzing how saturation influences photon-nucleus interactions and potential signatures indicating its presence within nucleon-nucleus and heavy nucleus-nucleus collisions.

Theoretical models predict that the most metal-poor stars in the universe should exhibit significant abundance variations, known as overabundance tails, relative to iron. However, observational data for stars with metallicities below -2.0 are scarce, and existing measurements for objects with [Fe/H] < -2.0 often display abundance spreads exceeding these predictions. This study investigates the potential causes of such widespread discrepancies in low-metallicity stars, specifically examining the roles of accretion and magnetic activity. By analyzing a sample of 113 metal-poor stars (with [Fe/H] < -2.0) from the APOGEE survey, we established a relationship between the abundance spread and iron abundance. Our findings reveal a substantial spread of 0.2 dex for the most iron-deficient stars, a magnitude significantly larger than the spread of 0.06 dex observed in extremely metal-poor (TMC) stars. To explain this result, we evaluated two primary hypotheses: first, that these stars are not genuine single entities but rather binary systems; second, that TMC overabundances are suppressed by magnetic activity. Employing Bayesian model selection, we determined that a combination of both mechanisms is required to account for the APOGEE data. Specifically, we conclude that approximately 50% of these objects are binaries, while magnetic activity suppression is responsible for the remaining cases.

This study examines the sensitivity of machine learning models to data transformations, such as scaling, using a toolkit designed to analyze linear, tree, and linear-model-based tree ensembles through principal component analysis (PCA). We apply this framework to financial data, leveraging individual investment behavior to forecast an individual's financial literacy score. Our analysis reveals that investment patterns are primarily driven by two principal components: risk aversion and financial knowledge. Furthermore, performance remains stable across various modeling and preprocessing approaches, indicating robust results that do not depend on specific data scaling techniques.

This paper proposes a novel framework for quantum machine learning built upon a Superconducting QUantum Interference Device (SQQUID). A SQQUID functions as a true quantum oscillator, offering an alternative to the qubit (two-level system) which acts as a discrete quantum particle. We demonstrate that the SQUID facilitates the implementation of core linear algebra operations essential for quantum learning algorithms. Specifically, we show that the eigenmodes of a SQUID can serve as ideal quantum neural network (QNN) units, while the corresponding eigenvectors constitute the ideal feature space. By configuring the QNN weights as a tunable magnetic flux and the training data as an initial coherent state, one can effectively execute the encoding, processing, and readout of that data. This approach is not only viable for executing standard quantum learning protocols but also accommodates the implementation of various machine learning algorithms.

This paper introduces and examines two pointwise submanifold types in a nearly contact manifold: the pointwise semi-slant submanifold and its distorted variant, the distorted distorted product pointwise semi-slant submanifold. For the former, we establish essential criteria for it to qualify as a pointwise slant submanifold, along with formulating its Christoffel symbols, curvature metrics, and deriving the Einstein equation. Regarding the latter structure, we identify the conditions under which it degenerates to a pointwise semi-slant submanifold, calculate its Gauss curvature, section, Ricci curvature, and sectional curvature components, and explicitly determine its specific solution set.

The current generation of low-background experiments, such as those in direct dark matter searches and those probing neutrinoless double beta decay, are increasingly sensitive to recoil events stemming from radioactive decay within the detector itself. These self-induced signals can potentially be tracked over time by analyzing the evolution of intrinsic color centers in the target material. This study details the color center analysis conducted within the 2018 campaign of the 1.3-tonne SuperCDMS single-gemini germanium detector. We explore how these color centers offer a pathway to quantify sub-thermal nuclear recoil energies arising from isotopes intrinsic to the device.

This study investigates how active colloids, which exhibit persistent motion driven by an internal energy source, behave in constant, linear activity gradients. We demonstrate that persistent motion causes the particles to migrate up these gradients. We establish a migration mechanism driven by the interaction between the particle's finite autocorrelation time of its activity and the spatial variation of the field, allowing for analytical predictions of the migration velocity. We also examine the role of particle shape and hydrodynamic boundary conditions, noting that while such factors can amplify migration speeds, active particles remain mobile in any non-uniform activity field.

The edge states of the fractional quantum Hall effect (FQHE) are governed by non-Abelian bosonic fields and their interactions with magnetons and electrons. Because these edges support both right- and left-propagating modes, they can be modeled as two distinct 1+1-dimensional bosonic field theories. This work aims to rigorously establish two theorems: first, that a magnetorotonic sequence of every order $n$ exists for both 1+1D theories, and second, that a spectral totality rule (analogous to the Boutroux identities in theory) governs the relationship between the modes of these two edge types. To prove the first theorem, we employ the Lax pair and its associated Zakharov-Shabat matrix, alongside an analysis of the nontrivial monodromy group generated at each FQHE level. For the second, we derive a set of identities we term "cyclemag," which mirror the structure of Boutroux conditions. These results hold for both rational and irrational FQHE systems, though their physical implications are more pronounced in the latter.

Clustering serves as a key component in the early detection of disease outbreaks on complex networks. This study introduces a new geometric clustering technique that identifies nodes belonging to the same transmission cluster by evaluating the distance between a node and a potential geometric boundary representing a disease outbreak. The approach was validated on various contact networks, including air traffic, university, and social networks, as well as in a geometric high-school contact network. Clustering performance was assessed using both synthetic and real-world outbreak scenarios. Additionally, the method was applied to a recent COVID-19 case at the University of Edinburgh, successfully isolating cases within a specific campus cluster and effectively distinguishing them from the broader population.

The point source removal method of the Planck Collaboration, known as X, relies on maximum likelihood (ML) mapping. This technique employs priors with infinite variance, theoretically allowing maps to remain unchanged while isolating point sources. However, our analysis reveals that this approach is not immune to residual biases in resulting maps. We demonstrate that these imperfections can be eliminated by redefining the initial distribution to possess finite variance, a change that simultaneously improves the precision of the point source catalog.

Communicative abilities are a defining trait of intelligence, yet agents capable of acquiring complex skills solely through high-level verbal goals in a visually grounded environment are relatively rare. This paper introduces visual grounding as a critical missing component in natural language-based reinforcement learning, demonstrating that the referential ambiguity of language is a valuable source of exploratory noise. We propose that this ambiguity should be harnessed to accelerate learning. To this end, we present a generation-based approach that selects the most appropriate noun phrase for an action description from a set of candidate options. After evaluating the method across three distinct environments, we find that while the unambiguous identification of objects is not always achieved, the system effectively boosts performance and scales effectively when dealing with lists of noun objects.

Quantum channel tomography is a critical task for developing quantum technologies. While the shadow tomography method proposed in 2019 is a powerful, efficient tool for estimating the characteristics of both quantum states and channels, its original formulation is restricted to completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) maps. In this work, we extend the shadow tomography approach to address arbitrary quantum channels, not limited to CPT maps, and demonstrate its utility in characterizing non-CPT operations. We apply this generalized method to the task of analyzing channels via process matrices, showing that the required number of experiments using the technique is significantly lower than traditional methods. Furthermore, we examine the specific scenario involving a single input and single output qubit, deriving a specific protocol and providing a theoretical framework for analyzing its data. Our experiments confirm the feasibility of this approach, revealing that the number of necessary measurements using the generalized shadow method is substantially reduced compared to standard techniques.

Additionally, we establish a resolved version of the so-called "Klee's Conjecture" regarding this Cheeger constant in non-overlapping convex sets in the plane with shared boundaries.

Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly recognized as a promising solution for diverse applications, ranging from high-speed data delivery and environmental monitoring to surveillance and disaster response. This paper introduces a novel algorithm, the Dynamic Speed Adjustment (DSA) method, which optimizes flight trajectories to maximize mission efficiency by allowing real-time velocity control based on dynamic constraints. The objective is to complete a defined sequence of tasks within a time limit, covering the minimum possible distance. The interplay between molecular conformation and electronic properties is a critical area of study. We report a detailed investigation into the temperature-dependent behavior of the fullerenes Sc2TbN@C80, specifically examining their interaction with the Ni(111) substrate via an h-BN buffer layer. Using a combination of in situ techniques—specifically ultrahigh vacuum (UHV) X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), angle-resolved photoemission (ARPES), and scanning tunneling microscopy (STM)—we analyzed the material across varying temperatures. Our findings reveal that Sc2TbN@C80@hBN transitions from a D5h symmetric form at room temperature to a C2v configuration at elevated temperatures above 350°C. Furthermore, the study elucidates the relationship between this conformational shift and the resulting changes in the material's electronic structure.

The Internet of Things (IoT) refers to the vast network of simple devices that communicate and exchange data. These IoT devices are characterized by their minimal computational power, limited memory, and small storage capacity. The growing popularity of IoT has driven significant research interest in securing these systems, yet many existing security solutions impose a heavy computational burden that exceeds the capabilities of low-power devices. This paper introduces a survey of lightweight algorithms and lightweight protocols. The work aims to guide future research by surveying current lightweight algorithms and protocols, analyzing their advantages and limitations, and demonstrating how they can be applied to secure IoT systems. This survey will also help researchers understand how to design and implement efficient security mechanisms that meet the strict resource constraints of IoT devices while providing robust protection against various cyber threats.

This study outlines a statistically rigorous method for determining the optimal number and configuration of measurements within an adaptive Ramsey sequence through sequential Bayesian trial formulation. We demonstrate that this approach enables the identification of optimal global parameters, including the specific count of measurements and their settings, while being executed via a "trial-and-error" procedure that utilizes results from actual experiments to inform subsequent steps. Additionally, we establish that this strategy is robustly effective for both the optimization and implementation of quantum sensors.

This study introduces a novel approach to measuring network centrality, Gromov Centrality (GOC), which is derived from the foundational concepts of metric geometry and utilizes novel metrics based on the triangle inequality surplus. By integrating these comprehensive distance metrics, the metric effectively uncovers the nuanced topological roles inherent within intricate networks. Notably, the analysis reveals a robust positive correlation between the Gromov Centrality and traditional centrality measures, underscoring its validity and practical value.

The variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) serves as the primary quantum algorithm for determining the ground state of molecular electronic structures. Nevertheless, its widespread application is constrained by its reliance on extensive qubit resources and its inability to sufficiently lower the energy of single-excitation states. To address these limitations, this work introduces an adaptive VQE framework that leverages tamm-dancoff qubit-excitation operators to demand fewer qubits and tackle the excitation state restriction. By employing this qubit-efficient qubit-excitation adaptive VQE on the N₂ molecule via classical hybrid calculations, this approach successfully converged to the exact ground state energy, achieving a result within 0.0002 eV of the non-relativistic full configuration interaction limit, using only 40% of the qubits necessary for a standard VQE implementation.

While standard autoencoders are often criticized for losing significant information during the bottleneck encoding phase, this paper introduces the "profound generative decoder" as a remedy. We demonstrate that this decoder possesses far greater representational capacity than a simple mapping function from representations to inputs. We further establish a powerful theoretical guarantee: given enough training data, the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) of this generative decoder, denoted as $g^*$, can recover the original data distribution defined by $p(x)$, even if the initial representations $z$ contain substantial information loss. By leveraging this robust estimator, representations learned via deep autoencoders can effectively reconstruct the true underlying data distribution $p(x)$, a capability that standard AE models lack. We also present a new unsupervised method for discovering semantic concepts, a task that is infeasible with standard AE representations. Finally, experimental results across unsupervised and supervised settings validate the effectiveness of this approach.

This work demonstrates that within the framework of synthetic differential geometry, there exists a single, unique (up to isomorphism) differential groupoid capable of serving as the groupoid of applications from a given smooth scheme to a smooth target. This result highlights the significance of the group-theoretic language, where the concept of a topological linkage space (groupoid) is the natural substitute for its classically related but less fundamental linked Lie group counterpart. Additionally, we establish that such groupoids are intrinsically path-connected—a natural generalization of the standard property found in Lie groups—and show that their global integral of vector fields is uniquely determined by the vector field itself and its associated differential equation, without requiring arbitrary choices of initial conditions.

The rising volume of data and computing power has made big data a vital driver of research and innovation across many fields. This trend is especially evident in life sciences, where it has spurred the creation of specialized cyberinfrastructures tailored to meet demands for efficient data processing and high-throughput storage. However, a significant hurdle remains: data sharing between these independent infrastructures is often difficult and inefficient. To address this, our group has developed the Biopharm Gateway (bGATE), a flexible gateway designed to support secure and streamlined access for both people and applications. This article offers an overview of bGATE's capabilities, implementation, and usage, highlighting its potential as a valuable resource for other cyberinfrastructure gateways within the bioinformatics domain.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) aims to determine the sentiment polarity of specific features within text. While deep learning models have achieved significant success in ABSA, they often struggle to uncover implicit sentiments that do not rely on the direct polarity of the target aspect. This framework integrates our proposed "DOMInICATION" dataset, which labels the sentiment polarity of numerous sentences within each context, along with the sentiment polarity of the focused aspects. DOMInICATION is the largest and most extensive collection of human-annotated ABSSA data to date. By training a transformer model on this rich annotation set, we demonstrate that it effectively captures the relationship between aspect implicit polarity and general sentiment. Furthermore, we combine this model with fine-tuning on existing ABSSA datasets to achieve state-of-the-art performance. Extensive testing on standard benchmarks confirms the superiority of DOMInIC over current state-of-the-art methods.

This paper investigates transmit and reflecting element configuration optimization for Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) within secure multiuser communication networks, accounting hardware impairments in both the transmitter (TX) and RIS. The objective is to ensure robust and reliable multiuser transmission, thereby reducing the likelihood of users receiving signals outside their intended access power levels. To achieve this, we derive a closed-form analytical bound for the probability that a user's received power deviates from the target threshold, incorporating both HW impairments and pathlosses. This bound is then utilized to design an efficient algorithm that jointly optimizes the TX's active gain and individual reflecting element efficiencies for every single-user link. Simulation outcomes confirm that the proposed method successfully reduces the transmission failure probability and outperforms existing state-of-the-art RIS designs lacking impairments or employing simplified models.

This study introduces XAIVC (Ability), an enhanced approach to maximizing contrastive returns within the value-based maximum contrastive learning (V3) framework. By leveraging hindsight summarization, XAIVC employs two specialized strategies: one utilizes the highest future values of trajectories to prioritize rewarding resampling, while both strategies assist in reassigning labels during relabeling. Empirical evaluations indicate that XAIVC surpasses the original V3 approach, as well as numerous other state-of-the-art algorithms. The Parker Solar Probe (PSP) mission has provided the first direct measurements of solar wind plasma and fields from within the Sun's corona, reaching a record distance of 9.86 solar radii ($R_{\odot}$). This dataset offers unprecedented insight into the solar wind's origin and evolution. This study analyzes the energy flux associated with the solar wind's turbulent fluctuations, or "solar breeze," as observed by PSP. Utilizing the "tangent-point" assumption, the research maps these in-situ readings to specific heights along Sun-synchronous magnetic field lines. The analysis reveals that the radial power spectral density of magnetic turbulence peaks at a frequency of approximately 0.03 Hz, with a corresponding peak scale length near 1.5 $R_{\odot}$. Furthermore, the "breeze" energy flow itself exhibits strong variability, peaking around 100 mV/m², roughly 1.75 $R_{\odot}$, and declining outward. These findings indicate that the turbulent breeze reaches its maximum intensity at altitudes significantly lower than where the magnetic field lines become taut. This behavior suggests the Sun's interior may host additional acceleration mechanisms for the solar wind, potentially driven by the amplification of turbulent fluctuations.

Neutron star mergers are thought to produce jets that are either collimated or wide-angle, depending on whether they draw energy from the spin of a black hole or from a falling-in, magnetized neutrino-cooled accretion disk. While such broad jets could explain the "wide-angle" gamma-ray bursts observed in long-duration events, we have not yet identified a mechanism capable of launching these outflows. In this study, we model the outflow from a magnetized disk using a two-dimensional hydrodynamic code and examine the resulting ejecta. We find that the ejecta display a highly asymmetric structure, featuring a central outflow alongside two off-axis components. The presence of these side jets contradicts the standard definition of a collimated or fully encompassing "pancake" wide-angle burst. Furthermore, we analyze the ejecta's morphology and energy spectra, revealing that the offset jets are significantly broader and more energetic than the central flow. These findings underscore the necessity of accounting for dynamical off-axis ejecta when interpreting the signatures of gravitational waves and r-process nucleosynthesis.

Features were classified as either distinct structures (DS) or diffuse features (DfF), the latter including tidal streams, dust lanes, and ellipses. Recent literature has demonstrated that large language models (LLMs) possess the ability to integrate external knowledge sources into their text generation without additional training. Building on this, we investigate how effectively LLMs can interpret specific visual information. Specifically, we examine the integration of visual controls—such as images and charts—to generate descriptive narratives. We introduce an automated evaluation framework that benchmarks the coherence of generated LLM texts against human annotations, focusing on Chroptify tasks where summaries describe images. Our results indicate that while current models struggle to create detailed visual descriptions, they successfully leverage visual input for control-based narrative generation. Furthermore, we assess various architectural designs and training strategies, identifying that models trained on visual-control pairing data outperform those trained solely on textual data. These findings suggest a promising path for enhancing LLM capabilities in multi-modal applications.

We introduce a modified RingCT variant that shrinks the digital signature on every single input within a transaction while keeping the signature size per output unchanged. By leveraging delegated signatures and utilizing new cryptographic methods based on bilinear pairings, this approach reduces the overall transaction volume. The space-efficient Delegated RingCT maintains identical levels of privacy and security relative to standard RingCT. Experimental analysis confirms the practicality of the system, showing that in current environments, the practical advantages emerge when a transaction involves ten or more inputs.

This article introduces a method for characterizing an accelerator's beam using spatial brightness profiles obtained from scanning devices. The approach relies on a parametric model of the beam's distribution, specifically the brightness per unit longitudinal and transverse space, which is derived from the Mott cross section of positron annihilation and measured via the device under study. We demonstrate that the fundamental distributions of two major particle sources—specifically those producing Gaussian characteristics and Donnelly-type beams from linear colliders—can be accurately and efficiently reconstructed using this technique. The method's robustness against experimental noise is evaluated, and the results are benchmarked against existing reconstruction algorithms. Furthermore, the work explores the application of this scan strategy to two proposed future facilities: a planned linear positron collider and a proposed high-luminosity electron collider at CEBAF. These studies aim to illustrate how the brightness map reconstruction can effectively analyze and beam characterize positron and electron beams in high-energy physics contexts.

We introduce a collaborative framework designed to create statistical models, such as deep neural networks, by leveraging shared knowledge across multiple agents. This approach addresses the high computational cost and extensive training data typically required, which are often burdensome for individual agents. We specifically address three scenarios: (1) sequential access to agent data, (2) simultaneous access to all agents' data, and (3) a decentralized setting where communication occurs only between the central model and individual agents, excluding agent-agent interaction. We develop a distributed gradient descent method to optimize the shared knowledge model, enabling personalized updates from locally available data. We also present a communication-efficient variant that significantly reduces the need for inter-agent dialogue. We provide theoretical convergence guarantees for the communication-efficient version and empirically demonstrate the advantages of this framework, particularly in terms of communication efficiency, across all three scenarios.

Training neural networks with quantized weights and activations allows for efficient deployment on edge devices with restricted resources, yet it frequently results in degraded accuracy compared to full-precision models. To address this, the study introduces AskwSGD, an algorithm designed to integrate quantization directly into the optimization process rather than applying it post-hoc. By simultaneously addressing two major limitations—non-monotonic landscape degradation and the lack of support for interval-based weight quantization—AskwSGD combines the benefits of a novel, previously unknown analytical framework with a novel, previously unknown analytical framework to improve upon these aspects. The method ensures that the average model performance does not decline over time and accommodates interval-quantization schemes. Experimental evaluations on standard benchmarks demonstrate that AskwSGD achieves superior results to both unmodified stochastic gradient descent and other anneared quantization strategies.

Soft robotics represents a dynamic and promising field within mechanical engineering, attracting substantial research interest driven by the unique advantages of soft actuators over traditional rigid components. However, the control of these soft systems poses significant challenges due to their non-linear, time-varying behavior. Consequently, this paper provides a comprehensive review of modeling methodologies aimed at overcoming these control hurdles. It examines the evolution from the initial hard-to-apply analytical models to modern finite element-based approaches, and critically analyzes the limitations, such as the need for precise material properties in kinematic models. Furthermore, this review outlines soft actuator modeling strategies, along with accompanying optimization techniques, and concludes by highlighting current gaps in the literature and suggesting future research directions.

Confirming facts within a database is a critical yet difficult task. While deep learning approaches have recently gained traction for solving this problem, existing methods are limited to text-free tables and fail to effectively handle complex queries involving multiple conditions. This study introduces a novel framework for table-based fact verification that integrates both textual and structural features. We propose a new strategy for decomposing tables into smaller segments to facilitate the creation of intermediate representations. Specifically, our approach employs sequence-to-sequence models to decompose tables into multiple sub-regions, which are then processed by a table encoder. This encoder generates a representation enriched with both textual and structural information, ultimately feeding into an attention mechanism that aggregates information from the entire table. Experimental results on a newly proposed, extensive benchmark demonstrate that this integration significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques.

Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (cGANs) are widely used to generate realistic images from continuous conditionings like text or images. However, this reliance on continuous inputs often results in unstable generated outputs. To address this, we introduce an approach to represent conditional information within a latent semantic space. A trained GAN learns this latent semantically space and acquires the embedding of specific conditions using an additional network tailored for that task. The target conditions are then approximated by incorporating a distributional offset into a point or region selected by a generator sampler. The outcome of the generation process is conditioned implicitly by modifying these latent regions. We empirically demonstrate that this method yields more consistent results compared to direct point sampling. Furthermore, we evaluate the approach against standard techniques using various offset distributions and find it achieves a superior balance of result quality and consistency.

Fully-Uniform Sampling (FUS) of layered structures is achieved by combining a rejection step with acceptance based on a contrast function. This study establishes the conditions under which any pair of FUS algorithms can be merged into a single FUS algorithm using the contrast function derived from their intersection. We introduce an infinite family of such dual-algorithm pairs where the two methods are identical except for how they handle layers of varying thickness. We also derive theoretical bounds for the performance efficiency of the resulting unified algorithm compared to the original dual pair. One specific instance of this family corresponds to the transition between Rejection (R) and Acceptance (A); merging them yields a unified FUS method, which is a variation of Acceptance-Rejection (AR). In this scenario, the optimal contrast function for the united AR is proven to be its contrast function itself. Furthermore, the study examines the contrast function of the united AR when applied to acceptance sampling, offering a generalized formulation of a previously proposed criterion by A. N. Boykin.

In reinforcement learning, gradient descent is frequently employed to tune model parameters by minimizing a specific loss function. To address this, we propose a framework for identifying and constructing loss functions by directly specifying their desired gradient properties. Validated through extensive RL experiments involving continuous and discrete actions as well as value estimation, our method demonstrates the ability to synple and effective loss functions tailored to specific needs.

The work presented examines $2+1$ flavor lattice QCD simulations across the range of baryon chemical potentials ($\mu_B$) from 0 to 0.8 fm$^{-1}$. These calculations, performed at temperatures ($T$) between 0.12 and 0.30 fm$^{-1}$, utilize gauge actions derived from the highly improved Schaefer action alongside improved lattice operators. The escalating demand for electricity has necessitated the deployment of offshore wind turbines in increasingly demanding, deep-water environments far from shore. To address the associated financial risks and operational uncertainties, there is an urgent need for highly accurate yet computationally efficient load prediction methods. This study introduces a novel statistical framework utilizing chained Gaussian processes (GP) to model the temporal evolution of offshore wind turbine loads. Unlike conventional approaches, this framework explicitly accounts for load non-stationarity and inter-tower load correlations. By integrating a stochastic process within the chain, the method also captures unmeasured external load excitation. The approach is validated using synthetic data from a two-tower configuration, demonstrating that a dual-chain GP structure achieves superior accuracy compared to single models. Furthermore, the investigation of correlations between tower currents and residual load errors confirms that the proposed GP chain effectively models cross-load correlations.

This paper details the examination of Twitter data concerning a specific tragic event in Izmir, Turkey. The authors analyze the temporal and spatial distribution of tweets, the demographics of users, and the relationships among them. The objective is to outline the fundamental techniques for leveraging social media for crisis management and disaster relief.

A group $G$ qualifies as $R_\infty$ under its nilpotent lower central series quotient if and only if each successive quotient $G/\gamma_{i+1}(G) : \gamma_i(G)$ exhibits this property. The authors establish that for a generalized solvable Hirsch-Howson (Baumslag-Solier) group, the property holds for the first such series segment precisely when the associated integer parameters satisfy specific arithmetic conditions. The paper further details the requisite conditions for higher stages of the series, providing a comprehensive characterization applicable to arbitrary levels in the lower central hierarchy.

A major challenge in experimental physics involves inferring hidden information from data collected over time. This work introduces a robust method for inverting time-resolved data by applying forward-optimization within a trajectory framework. We demonstrate that this approach enables the reliable reconstruction of stochastic trajectories of individual particles from noisy single-molecule observations. Notably, the optimized paths remain resistant to the statistical fluctuations inherent in the measurement record, allowing it to effectively separate distinct populations even with limited data samples. This technique is applicable to a broad range of fields, including single-molecule biophysics, where it can accurately resolve dynamic information from single realizations, and more general physics and chemistry problems involving the analysis of reduced phase-space data.

Naturalistic Driving Data (NDD) serves as a valuable asset for developing and evaluating models in autonomous driving, offering driving scenarios that are more diverse than those found in standard test sets. Nevertheless, real-world driving scenarios are highly intricate, and current NDDs often lack sufficient detail to support rigorous driving scenario recognition. Consequently, this study introduces SceNDD, a comprehensive naturalistic driving dataset designed to facilitate driving scenario recognition. The dataset was gathered from 12 vehicles across 11 cities in China, featuring 1,000 hours of high-fidelity recordings from 2021. It incorporates multi-modal data—including camera feeds, high-resolution maps, and precise positioning and tracking data for the ego-vehicle and surrounding agents. Furthermore, we propose a novel framework for scenario recognition that leverages structural differences among scenarios. Experimental results indicate that utilizing this proposed method along with the provided annotations allows for significantly improved performance in driving scenario recognition.

We propose a new class of local conformal field theories, known as Reflected CFTs, designed to model dynamics at domain walls separating or defects within broader CFT frameworks. These theories operate by restricting standard conformal families to specific subcollections determined by representation restrictions on a special reflected subalgebra, the dynamics of which are governed by modular data. Specifically, Reflected CFTs exhibit tensor categories as both their chiral and right-moving sectors, facilitating the analysis of central charges and the construction of concrete examples through Wess-Zumino-Novikov-Wess (WZW) models. In doing so, we establish a direct link between the chiral content of a local CFT and its corresponding chiral theory, with reflected cases representing particular subclasses. Furthermore, while boundary and interface CFT classifications often rely on g-matrices, our study introduces the concept of reflected CFTs alongside their specific g-functions, which are integral to calculating the Renyi entropy of these systems.

Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) have emerged as a promising technology for enhancing 5G/6G mobile networks. This paper investigates channel estimation in RIS-assisted Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) systems that suffer from two specific impairments: inadequate Cyclic Prefix (CP) length and defective hardware components. The analysis focuses on scenarios where the uplink training sequences are projected by the RIS over a downlink data channel, creating an asymmetric uplink-downlink relationship caused by hardware flaws and insufficient CP. To address these challenges, we propose an Enhanced Linear Autoencoder (ELM) based channel estimation scheme. This method operates without the need for an extended CP or additional pilot symbols. Instead, it directly estimates the channel matrix from the received time-domain data, leveraging the inherent properties of ELMs. Simulation results demonstrate that the suggested approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques under the specified hardware limitations and CP constraints.

The work establishes a rigorous framework for quantifying the total energy exchange between a particle and its environment within energy-coupling-cycling (EEC) protocols. This framework enables non-intrusive measurements of free energy and dissipation while ensuring compliance with thermodynamic limits, as the integral fluctuation theorem (IFTE) is derived and a method for calculating measurement costs is proposed. The study further explores the connection between single-energy assessment IFTEs and thermodynamic uncertainty relations (TURs), demonstrating that reducing total dissipation can be achieved by minimizing the coupling strength between particle and environment. Additionally, it is shown that IFTEs remain valid even when the environment is not initially in thermal equilibrium, provided the initial state is sufficiently generic. Finally, numerical simulations are performed on a periodically driven harmonic oscillator to validate these theoretical findings.
By examining $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons within a nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ framework, we derive deformation conditions and identify the associated linear conditions.

The current global spread of the highly contagious SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus has prompted numerous nations to prioritize developing tools that facilitate the containment of the disease. Among these efforts, a key focus is on security and privacy-preserving technologies designed specifically for health-related applications. This study evaluates the confidentiality of two prominent contact tracing mobile applications used in Brazil: Zonda and Corona Warn. By analyzing the source code of these applications, we identified that the cryptographic keys utilized for computing risk levels are stored in unencrypted form on the device's memory. Consequently, attackers could exploit this flaw to compromise user data, including phone numbers, IP addresses, and location histories. We substantiated these findings through a practical attack demonstration. To mitigate such risks, we recommend the adoption of the Android Keystore system, which offers a secure environment for key storage.

Quantum neural networks (QNNs) are a developing field, yet questions regarding the necessity of quantum computing to operate these networks remain unanswered. This study introduces a specific type of quantum architecture that allows classical data to be processed by them. We demonstrate a hybrid approach where quantum networks are integrated with classical networks to create an end-to-end model that functions entirely without requiring quantum resources for training or inference. Our research indicates that this model surpasses classical benchmarks in image classification accuracy. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical framework for establishing lower bounds on its classification precision.

We have developed a tool that generates a shallow embedding of C within ACL2, capable of producing ACL2 code corresponding to almost any legal ACL2-based program. This tool serves as a code creation aid capable of handling a wide variety of legal C code, allowing users to specify a single high-level ACL2 program and automatically generating the necessary transliteration into both equivalent ACL2 implementations and their underlying proofs of correctness. Although the tool operates by treating C code essentially as unstructured text, it is highly capable, having successfully processed C programs comprising several thousand lines.
