This paper explores machine learning techniques within algebraic topology, with a particular emphasis on persistent homology, and identifies several areas of relevance for physics. First, we detail how to construct a persistence homology graph neural network (PHGNN) designed to predict labeled data by learning topological features, and we demonstrate its successful application in two machine learning challenges within condensed matter physics. Second, we outline a novel density functional theory framework based on this PHGNN. Finally, we discuss the conceptual foundations of the method and its broader implications for physics.

Using the nonrelativistic quark-extended framework, $J/\psi$ angular distributions in $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\eta_c,\chi_{cJ}$ processes are analyzed at next-to-leading order in $v_c$. These calculations incorporate both one-loop self-energy diagrams for vector and axial-vector mesons alongside $s$-channel unitarity constraints, with results also provided for $W$ terms. Furthermore, we assess the influence of nonfactorizable contributions, which are expected to be the dominant source of nonzero $W$ terms, on the angular distributions.

This paper investigates how user-friendly end-to-end encryption (E2EE) protocols can be made more accessible to enthusiastic casual signal users. We conducted a study with 16 participants to assess their understanding of authentication mechanisms, specifically focusing on PINs and QR codes. Our findings indicate that while users value privacy, their understanding of E2EE and associated PINs remains limited; many fail to recognize that a PIN secures a specific conversation or that a compromised PIN could allow an attacker to decrypt past messages. To bridge this gap, we propose an enhanced security model that incorporates a "security state" to clarify PIN functions and suggest future research directions. We anticipate this approach will better equip users to manage their security and foster more informed decision-making.

A new, streamlined, and highly precise method for calculating the instantaneous-to-annual solar-energy distribution via Gaussian quadrature is introduced. This approach integrates analytical exactness with computational efficiency, achieving superior accuracy in modeling solar-energy accumulation compared to earlier algorithms. Specifically, it surpasses the traditional solar-energy Gaussian quadrature (SEGQ) method by incorporating a transformation into linear solar-energy time intervals. This adjustment significantly reduces integration errors and enhances overall performance. Furthermore, calculations utilizing the solar-energy Gaussian quadrature (SEQ) method require only 10 nodes to precisely determine the instantaneous annual solar-energy distribution, regardless of whether the input data represents discrete measurements or continuous time-series records.

This paper introduces ViViT, a compact curvature estimator for both closed and open curves that leverages a matrix's reduced structure within a generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) framework. Specifically, it targets the closed closed form of GGN for two-dimensional closed curves and its extended structure for general open lines. By utilizing the reduced architecture of GGN, the method constructs a new, efficient algorithm for computing mean curvature with second-order accuracy, capable of real-time implementation on closed curves. Furthermore, the curvature estimates are demonstrated to remain stable regardless of variations in sampling density or initial discretization quality.

In many major world languages, nouns are assigned a grammatical gender that influences the morphological marking of associated words. This study investigates whether such a system shapes the mental representations of nouns, specifically examining whether the two primary gender categories in Spanish, masculine and feminine, influence language processing differently. To address this, we analyzed reaction time data from 1,000 native Spanish speakers as they completed a task requiring the verification of adjectives paired with male- or female-gendered nouns. Our results indicate that while mass nouns and those denoting human males are processed more rapidly than other concepts, these semantic factors also carry a stronger grammatical gender signal than do objects. These findings have significant implications for the debate regarding the grammatical status of gender in linguistics.

We demonstrate that for an arithmetic group, the following conditions are equivalent: the group contains a free subgroup, and both the group and its finite dimensional universal cover are charmable. Building on this, we define an arithmetic group as rigid when its finite dimensional universal cover is charmable; notably, all hyperbolic and nonuniformly lattices are shown to be charmable. Furthermore, if an arithmetic group is neither hyperbolic nor a uniform lattice, it is not charmable, and thus does not contain a free subgroup. Our investigation relies heavily on the concept of charmability, a concept derived from quasi-isometric topology and previously utilized by Rieck and Thomas to characterize nonhyperbolicity in certain finitely presented groups.

Object pose estimation is essential for various computer vision applications, including object detection, tracking, and reconstruction. Nevertheless, current methods typically necessitate training on substantial quantities of class-specific labeled object data. This paper introduces zero-shot class-level object pose estimation, a technique that avoids reliance on per-class training data. We propose a novel framework that leverages language models to derive pose information from object descriptions. This approach is implemented by training a pose encoder to generate pose vectors encoded within natural language descriptions of poses, alongside a language-augmented vector quantizer capable of retrieving these latent vectors from the encoded zero-shot class data data based on language queries. Extensive testing on the Pascal Context dataset demonstrates the model's effectiveness, achieving an average maximum average precision (AP) of 10.5% across 20 classes without any class-specific pose training.

Predicting traffic flow is a critical component of intelligent transportation systems. While deep learning methods have recently gained prominence, they typically struggle with sparse data environments due to their heavy reliance on extensive historical information. This paper introduces a novel framework that leverages similarity to address traffic flow prediction specifically within sparse data conditions. This approach utilizes a similarity graph to identify traffic time series that are comparable, transforming the original prediction task into one of similarity transfer. Consequently, a forecasting model is developed by transferring knowledge from these similar transferred sequences. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques across multiple urban datasets.

This paper introduces VACA, a new class of variational graph autoencoders designed for structure learning with intervention and counterfactual queries. Distinguished from existing methods, VACA does not require a separate model for interventional or counterfactual distributions; instead, it employs a single generative model capable of producing both observed data and targets of interest. This adaptability allows for the estimation not only of probabilities for interventions or counterfactuals but also of their associated generative mechanisms. The approach learns a generative graph structure from unobserved interventional or counterfactual targets while strictly adhering to Markov and independence properties inherent to the data. To achieve this, we define a novel variational objective that can be maximized using standard stochastic variational inference. Our empirical results demonstrate that VACA outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in both generative quality and generative world simulation, exhibiting superior scalability when dealing with high-dimensional latent representations.

The REAL-time Transient Collection (RTC) project, led by the SKA Outreach and Transient Collaboration, seeks to establish open, real-time transient science pipelines for global use. At LOFAR's Netherlands array, the project's success relies on the Irish RealTA backend, which is currently the only such system operating outside the Netherlands. This system was developed by the Irish LOFAR team, led by the author, in close cooperation with the SKA Transient Collaboration. This article provides a high-level overview of the system's architecture and software, and it presents a scientific analysis of the initial transient data collected during its first 100 days of operation. This evidence demonstrates RealTA's capability to detect a diverse range of transient events, including the Crab pulsar, FRBs 190425M and 190720, the FRB 190529 burst train, and several fast radio bursts. Additionally, the system has identified numerous pulsars, both previously known and newly discovered, as well as a significant number of FRBs, some of which have been reported in prior literature and others which are novel findings.

This article reviews how machine learning algorithms have been applied to solve practical challenges within the field of metrophotonic systems. We begin by examining machine learning's fundamental principles and its connection to physical laws. Next, we explore algorithms and their training processes, demonstrating the transformative potential of metaphotonics—leveraging the integration of intelligent machines and metamaterials. Finally, we outline future directions and the prospective evolution of metaphotonics.

This study introduces a comprehensive dataset comprising 2,000 motion pictures from the years 2000 to 2020, featuring 20 distinct pre-release attributes. The research aims to analyze how these traits influence box office revenue. The methodology employs two complementary approaches: first, it examines individual impacts through non-parametric statistics, and second, it assesses both single and combined effects by utilizing linear regression, random forest, and gradient boosting regression tree models. The analysis reveals that while script quality is the single most significant predictor of financial success, attributes such as genre, language, and release month also play substantial roles. Additionally, experimental results confirm that strategically selecting a combination of features can enhance the forecast accuracy of linear models. The study concludes with recommendations for future research directions.

This study demonstrates that the high-frequency voltage oscillations caused by renewable energy sources can be mitigated through the strategic deployment of auxiliary frequency regulation services. The analysis utilizes a DC power flow model incorporating area coupling, inductive power loss, and area-average voltage dynamics. This framework reveals that the system's small-signal behavior is governed by a coupled set of coupled first-order differential equations and second-order ordinary differential equations. The authors derive an analytical solution for this model, which indicates that active regions participating in auxiliary frequency regulation can significantly enhance system stability. The optimal configuration for these services is determined by solving an optimization problem designed to minimize the maximum power deviation across the network. The findings are validated using numerical simulations based on a modified IEEE 118-bus system.

This paper introduces a framework designed to model and analyze large-scale cyber-physical systems composed of interconnected networks. Leveraging concepts from network science, we mathematically derive the conditions for a given system to remain secure, while also developing a computational method to quantify its resilience. We further propose an intelligent strategy that identifies which specific connections to add in order to maximize system resilience, testing this approach on physical network models and extensive real-world datasets. Finally, we outline a comprehensive plan to validate this methodology through practical experiments.

This paper is the second in a series and explores how to model UV excess in Blazar Emission using a Monte Carlo method. Building on the results in Paper I, a new model is proposed that utilizes a non-relativistic, external-Compton scattering scenario to explain the broad UV excess observed in blazars. This approach is particularly attractive because it avoids the complexities of calculating photon scattering cross-sections for relativistic sources. By applying this model to UV excess data from three famous blazars—PKS 1424+22, OJ 287, and 3C 279—this paper confirms that relativistic effects are unnecessary to explain the UV excess in 3C 279 and that a blazar's UV excess can be attributed to the high-energy photon field of the supermassive black hole. This finding supports the hypothesis that supermassive black holes emit soft X-rays and gamma rays. These results validate Paper I's hypothesis that Black Hole UV Emission (BH-UV) is a viable model for blazar spectra. However, the hypothesis cannot yet explain the UV excess in OJ 287, suggesting that additional factors, such as accretion disc emission, must be considered. Finally, the implications of these results for future research are briefly discussed.

The core objective of this work is to develop a technique for the analytic continuation of surface potentials across complex topographies. This is achieved by introducing a novel multipole formulation designed to handle general twisted and turned boundaries. By defining the surface potential as a linear combination of functions that are simultaneously continuous and differentiable along the boundary, we enable a variable parameterization of the boundary itself. Through this approach, we derive an expression for both real and complex (including twisted-turn configurations) boundary representations suitable for separating surface potentials into distinct boundary element components. Consequently, we demonstrate that the divergence of these locally defined multipoles can be expressed as a combination of the basis functions representing different boundary segments. This separation facilitates the calculation of surface potentials anywhere within volume exclusion zones.

We introduce a digital approach to distinguish between the symmetric pure states within the fully antisymmetric subspace of $N$ qubits. This method relies on measuring the number of particles occupying a specific set of modes using local particle-number measurements. By selecting local dimensions sufficiently large, one can isolate symmetric pure states into distinct output distributions. Our findings demonstrate that the detection error probability decays exponentially with the number of utilized resources. Additionally, we establish that the optimal number of particles to measure, denoted as $k$, must satisfy the condition $1 \leqslant k \leqslant O(\log N)$, and we validate this through the analysis of specific cases.

Baryon creation is examined through the quantized breakage of helical QCD filaments. In this model, surface tension drives the formation of new loop ends resembling virtual pions, which subsequently capture color-triplet string fragments to form baryons. Baryons are depicted as three strings tethered to a central anchor point; as the loop fragments and the strings recoil with high kinetic energy, they fragment further into lighter hadrons and ultimately into free high-momentum baryons. The resulting baryon generation rates align well with experimental data from high-luminosity collisions.

The Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMSI) on the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) has been continuously capturing images of the Sun's disk since 2010. These data allow for the calculation of travel times, which serve as a diagnostic for sound speed variations. A persistent issue with this method is that active regions (ARs) generate anomalies in travel times that are indistinguishable from those caused by internal solar structures. To address this, we have developed a novel technique to identify ARs based on the travel time perturbations they induce. By cross-validating with independent SDO data, we have determined that these perturbations originate from ARs and their surrounding areas, where the sound speed is elevated by approximately 0.05% to 0.1%. Given that such sound speed increases are linked to enhanced plasma flows, we propose that the observed travel time anomalies result from the presence of these horizontal plasma movements.

The CMB represents only the most long-wavelength and earliest phase of cosmic structure formation. In contrast, the frequency bands of the Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) network are capable of detecting potential physical processes that may have occurred after the CMB era, specifically primordial gravitational fields. This study investigates signal signatures from a stochastic gravitational background generated by a stochastic vector field during radiation domination. The analysis reveals that the resulting GW spectral density scales as $N_{\rm CDM}^2$, where $N_{\rm CDM}$ is a parameter related to the vector field's initial amplitude. The signal strength is found to be comparable to or stronger than existing PTA observations across a wide range of scales, offering a novel search avenue for vector fields that are distinct from standard inflationary models.

This study investigates a new hybrid model designed to enhance vector-based cross-lingual information retrieval (CBIR) performance. Leveraging the extensive pre-training of multilingual models, the research demonstrates how the CBIR domain can harness both interactive and non-interactive benefits for machine translation (MT) and retrieval operations. Consequently, the authors introduce a hybrid CBIR framework that combines these translation approaches. Empirical results indicate that the proposed hybrid model outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods, achieving significant improvements in the TREC 12 Cross-Language track, specifically surpassing the best existing systems by 3.33% and 2.18% in Map and Pointwise Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG) metrics, respectively.

This paper evaluates both design-based and model-based techniques for generating small-area estimates within a low-and middle-income country context. A dataset comprising household-level socio-economic and health indicators from the 2016/17 Uganda Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) serves as the basis for analysis. Focusing on Uganda's 135 districts, our objective is to develop and contrast estimation approaches for two specific variables: household wealth and the prevalence of under-five mortality. A key challenge in this analysis is the extremely limited number of observations per district, stemming from the DHS multi-stage sampling architecture. To address this data scarcity, we employ Bayesian hierarchical small-area estimation frameworks that integrate external covariate data. These data are drawn from the 2015/16 Uganda Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS4), which offers richer detail across additional variables than the original DHS.

This paper introduces a continuous-variable framework for modeling quantum reward scenarios, distinct from traditional models that employ discrete outcomes. The analysis derives a continuous equivalent of Kelly's utility function and establishes a corresponding continuous-variable Kelly wagering equation within the quantum realm. Additionally, the study examines the asymptotic behavior of this utility function and determines the specific conditions under which a closed-form analytical solution exists. The methodology is ultimately validated through a illustrative example.

The rare decay process $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ represents a significant test of the Standard Model and a sensitive probe for new physics phenomena. Although this process is forbidden in the non-vanishing case of tree-level interactions under the Standard Model, it can proceed via loops. The LHCb collaboration recently presented initial measurements of this event. In this study, we perform a comprehensive analysis of the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^+$ decay event, including the angular distribution and its correlation with time-reversal invariance. The results are then compared with the Standard Model framework and various scenarios involving new physics to determine their implications.

The formation of planets relies on dust coagulation within a disk that forms alongside a young star. While disks are standard companions to stars, their origin remains unclear. This study investigates the formation of disks around pre-stellar cores during their gravitational collapse. We analyze a prestellar core modeled with a prestellar cloud, utilizing 3D Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) to simulate the dust-to-gas ratio. Our findings indicate that dust coagulation is unlikely to occur within the prestellar core, as radial expansion and rotation are insufficient to generate a significant velocity gradient necessary for planetesimal formation. Instead, angular momentum is transported outward, creating a disk with a dust-to-gas ratio of approximately 10⁻², distinct from the 10⁻³ ratio in the prestellar core. This disk is characterized by a high dust-to-gas ratio, a dense midplane, and a thick structure. Consequently, the research concludes that disk formation is a primary outcome of pre-stellar core collapse, rather than being linked to dust coagulation processes.

Atmospheric emission and scattering cause a discrepancy between the light received from an astronomical object and that from its background, a signal that enables atmospheric characterization via on-sky data. This process involves comparing telescope observations with synthetic reference data to retrieve specific atmospheric properties. This study utilizes the ATMO model to characterize the atmosphere of HD 189733b, leveraging the model's ability to reproduce high-quality spectra from Hubble Space Telescope data. Our analysis employs two techniques: a best-fit method that compares synthetic spectra against Hubble spectra to derive an atmospheric structure, and a retrieval method that simultaneously fits multiple HD 1897333b datasets to determine atmospheric properties. These findings are then used to test a water-rich atmosphere model for HD 189733b.

This work introduces a novel statistical series model designed to capture long-term dependencies in multi-temporal data while maintaining statistical efficiency through the use of deep learning. We propose a deep learning architecture that utilizes multiple convolutional layers to analyze the series, with their weights parameterized by a hierarchical Bayesian model. To mitigate overfitting and enhance model interpretability, we incorporate sparsity constraints within the deep learning components. Furthermore, we develop an efficient inference procedure based on the variational inference approach to enable the scalable fitting of these complex models. Empirical results across both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior predictive performance compared to existing state-of-the-art alternatives.

This note offers a proof of the most powerful compactness theorem using Pontryagin duality principles, while also establishing a connection between the for/and-not operators within classical logic and these two operators [designated, negated]. Additionally, it introduces "steast" logic, a variant that employs only the designated and/or operators alongside their inverse, and demonstrates the equivalence of its compactness properties to those of classical logic. The discussion also reveals an interplay between this new logical framework, the theory of groups, and Pontryagin duality.

Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning approach that trains distributed datasets across multiple clients without exchanging raw data, relying instead on the server to iterate model updates. Equity Considerations are essential in decision-making, particularly when prioritizing vulnerable groups over others. This research introduces an Equity-aware Federated Learning (EFEP) framework, modeled as Markov Decision Process (MDP), to guide servers in selecting client subsets for update based on their equity impact. The proposed method incorporates Differential Privacy (DP) within an iterative selection mechanism. By leveraging DP's privacy-preserving properties, the algorithm ensures that the chosen client set remains statistically robust and privacy-secure across server iterations. We demonstrate that this approach can be realized through both post-processing and post-collection privacy techniques while maintaining statistical consistency. Furthermore, we establish an asymptotic optimality guarantee for the server's long-term strategic selection of equity-conscious updates.

We introduce a supersymmetric minimal model featuring an extra $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetry, which can be realized by gauging a subgroup of $R$-symmetry within an extended R-parity violating (RPV) Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model extension. This framework allows for two distinct phenomenological scenarios: one where the dark matter (DM) candidate is mediated via $t$-channel exchange involving right-handed Majorana neutrinos ($n_{RM}$) and second where the standard RPV $t$-channel proceeds via a neutral scalar or vector boson ($\chi$ or $Z'$). In both cases, precision electroweak observability, Higgs sector constraints, and direct and indirect dark matter constraints are satisfied, allowing for viable parameter regions at TeV scales. Notably, the $Z'$ resonance could be discovered through its decay into a pair of right-handed neutrinos at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), while the $Z'$ resonance itself might be visible in its resonant production of a Higgs pair.

The approach is grounded in the premise that the system throughput can be effectively optimized by identifying a specific pattern in the power allocation strategies of the energy receivers. This study reports a half-life determination for $^{186}$Hg, achieved by analyzing the total counts of $^{186}$Hg activity following its decay to $^{186}$Tl and subsequent transition to $^{182}$Pb. We introduce a novel approach for designing controllers based on learning the optimization of Lyapunov functions, enabling the synthesis of a single controller that simultaneously masters multiple tasks. This method is designed to function effectively with limited data and side information, a context where the connection between different tasks is explicitly utilized to facilitate cross-task inference. By employing a data-driven framework, the current work demonstrates the ability to attain and switch between locomotion and flight capabilities. Specifically, data from one task can enhance the learning of another, while the inclusion of side information—such as a predefined relationship between tasks—significantly accelerates the convergence of the controller. This capability is validated through a simulation involving the mastery of walking, swimming, and flying. Furthermore, the study addresses the inverse problem by using learned multi-task controllers to derive appropriate Lyapunov functions for each specific objective.
We establish and verify various Ward identities within the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory, building upon the algebraic framework outlined in \cite{WardToda}.

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) excel at producing high-quality images, yet they struggle with few-shot scenarios due to their inability to leverage prior knowledge about object characteristics. While recent approaches like the Relation Networks with GANs (RNG) and Gaussian RNGs (GRG) attempt to harness object properties for classification, they have yet to fully address few-shot challenges. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel model termed the GAN with Relation Triplets (GRTN). This framework integrates object triples into the adversarial training process through a specialized loss function. Our approach involves training an RGB-based discriminator to assess the plausibility of image-object-class triplets, followed by a refined generator that synthesizes coherent triples rather than isolated pictures. We further enhance the model using a metric learning component to boost classification accuracy. Our experiments, conducted on mini-ImageNet and few-shot CUB datasets, demonstrate significant performance gains over prior methods.

Phase-free quantum key distribution utilizing coherent states has been previously proposed, but the lack of experimental validation has been a significant limitation. This paper introduces a phase-free Dual-field Quantum Key Distribution (D-F-QKD) scheme. In this approach, orthogonal coherent pulses are transmitted through separate channels to a quantum detector, and the phase partitioning coherence produced by the interference of these signals enables secure quantum key generation without the need for phase stabilization. Furthermore, the D-F-QKD protocol demonstrates that secure communication is achievable even if the transmitter emits coherent packets with a very low average photon count.

This paper investigates C*-algebras generated by isometries acting on the Hilbert and Bergman spaces. In many instances, these algebras turn out to be Toeplitz algebras corresponding to specific matrices. We derive graph representations of these structures to analyze their K-theory, ultimately characterizing their ideal lattices as Toeplitz maximal.

Current lexical object detection (LexOBJ) methods typically rely on static, manually labeled datasets, which restricts their ability to generalize to new vocabularies. Conversely, while leveraging pseudo-word embeddings has shown promise for enabling access to open lexicons, these methods often suffer from degraded performance due to inaccuracies in bounding box annotations. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel open LexOBJ framework utilizing the "pseudo bounding-box" annotation. This approach involves training an object detector using word-level masks to refine character-level segmentation, followed by calculating the mean bounding box for each word to serve as the final "pseudo" annotation. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on four out of five open-LexOBj benchmarks, surpassing previous approaches by an average increase of 3.3% in box localization accuracy.

Neural Architecture Search (NAS) seeks to automatically discover high-performance neural networks, yet the vast architectural design space and prohibitive training costs remain significant hurdles. This paper investigates interference among subtasks within NAS algorithms, a phenomenon that distorts search trajectories and constrains discovery. We identify that interference arises from two sources: (1) the inherent structure of the architecture representation, and (2) the suboptimality of the search algorithm. To address these issues, we propose two remedies. First, we demonstrate that subtasks can be decoupled when using operational sequences as architecture functions, thereby eliminating much of the interference. Second, we introduce a search strategy that mitigates interference by redefining the objective function to account for task interactions. Experimental results across multiple benchmarks validate that our methods enhance algorithmic performance, uncovering superior architectures that were previously undiscovered.

Excessive data collection in the digital era has heightened the necessity for efficient, high-quality time-series analysis. Traditional methods, which concentrate on forecasting, often overlook critical factors like seasonality, trends, and anomalies. This limitation is particularly problematic when dealing with sensitive data, such as time-series with irregular observations, missing values, or those that do not conform to standard models. This paper introduces a novel framework for Time-Series Examination that addresses the gaps in conventional approaches. We present a comprehensive R package, named `theft`, featuring a broad spectrum of tests designed to validate assumptions and enhance the accuracy of prediction models. These tools enable the detection of weak or strong seasonality, non-linearity, trends, irregularities, and both classical and contextual outliers. Furthermore, the package offers capabilities for estimating optimal lags and selecting appropriate models. We validate our approach through extensive experiments on real-world datasets, demonstrating that our methodology yields superior outcomes compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

The field of machine translation has advanced significantly over the last few decades, yielding multiple state-of-the-art systems. Consequently, distinguishing between the reliability of various machine translation (MT) systems has become a pressing issue. This study proposes a Bayesian framework for assessing the reliability of MT systems. The model incorporates two primary parameters: performance, measured using the BLEU score, and consistency, defined as the probability that a system correctly outperforms a baseline. We evaluate our method's performance against a conventional approach utilizing a benchmark dataset of four MT systems. Experimental results indicate that our proposed method achieves greater accuracy in identifying the most reliable system compared to traditional techniques.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have proven superior to fully connected networks (FCNs) across numerous computer vision tasks. This study investigates the underlying reasons for this performance advantage, hypothesizing that CNNs succeed because they inherently discard unhelpful features. We introduce a new method called Lifting, which identifies and removes redundant attributes from FCNs to enhance their performance. Through an examination of the connection between feature selection and network performance, we demonstrate that in many scenarios, the optimal strategy involves selecting a subset of the initial attributes rather than all of them. Furthermore, we show that when using early attributes as foundation layers, CNNs tend to select more widely distributed attributes compared to the adjacent ones. These findings offer valuable insights for selecting features and highlight a key distinction between CNNs and FCNs, clarifying why the convolutional architecture prevails over fully connected architectures.

This paper introduces a generalized utility function designed to capture investor preferences for lottery tickets, incorporating both an increasing scale valuing monetary gains and a nonlinear component valuing anticipated pleasure. That nonlinear element peaks at an optimal level of anticipated profit; consequently, the ticket's total anticipated worth rises rapidly when ownership is scarce but plateaus and eventually declines when the likelihood of owning them is high. This behavior indicates a strategy shift: as anticipation of possession rises, the price willing to be paid for an additional ticket should fall, and the potential for strategic cycling—buying and disposing—to generate wealth becomes increasingly viable. The proposed utility function aligns with both established economic theories and observed market dynamics, such as the inverse relationship between prices and demand along with the rise of repeat purchases and sell orders.

This paper details our strategy for the NeurIPS 2022 Challenge on Visual Domain Adaptation. To address generalization across various scenarios, we developed multiple architectures tailored to distinct domains, each optimized using adversarial losses and gradient reversal units alongside methods like feature freezing and ensemble techniques. Furthermore, we implemented a two-stage approach for the multi-task setting: first, models were pre-trained individually per task; second, a final model was constructed by aggregating the representations learned in those tasks.

Dimensionality reduction techniques are vital for managing high-dimensional datasets, yet many existing approaches fail to account for the geometric characteristics of the input space. This limitation is particularly acute for spherical data found in domains like directional information, where items are represented as unit vectors. This study examines t-SNE, a widely adopted non-linear dimensionality reduction method, specifically regarding its application to spherical data represented as unit vectors. Our analysis demonstrates that applying t-SNE to such spherical data results in sub-optimal outcomes because these geometric nuances are ignored. To address this, we introduce t-SNE specifically adapted for unit vectors, incorporating two key modifications: first, the substitution of Euclidean distance with angular distance to respect the intrinsic geometry of the sphere, and second, the replacement of the cross-entropy loss function with a vector-based objective. Our experimental results indicate that this proposed method consistently outperforms the original t-SNE and other state-of-the-art SNE variants across multiple real-world Spherical datasets.

This study examines zero-range attractive impurity-Fermi gas interactions within two dimensions using the fermion polaron framework of large fluctuation Monte Carlo methods, which incorporate a coupling to an explicit polaron degree of freedom representing the impurity. By analyzing the impurity's self-energy, we determine that the fermion-exchange hole fails to prevent an impurity-induced two-particle collapse, leading to an unstable non-interacting ground state. Consequently, a finite energy separation exists between this non-interacting ground level and the lowest order ground level of the collpsed cluster. The calculated ground state energy, when expressed in terms of the gas's Fermi energy, aligns well with recent determinations from Quantum Monte Carlo simulations.

We introduce a hybrid analog-digital approach designed to efficiently simulate fermionic many-body systems, leveraging the capabilities of current noisy, intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) processors. By utilizing the hardware-efficient ansatz, this method embeds fermionic operators within the native gate set of existing quantum architectures. The proposed strategy employs digital gates solely to execute fermionic operator projections, eliminating the exponential scaling costs associated with full digital simulations. We demonstrate the method's efficacy through the quantum equation of state of unitary gases and finite-temperature magnetic susceptibility calculations for the one-dimensional Hubbard model.

Specifically, a generic system within this group is characterized by a curve $X$ of genus $g$ and a collection of $n+1$ distinct points on it, where $n$ represents a non-negative integer. A key structural feature of these systems is their collection of monodromy representations into the special linear group $SL(n,\mathbb{C})$.

While classical methods by Katzarkov-Liu-Nitsan established that the moduli space of such generically defined representations is smooth, complete, and possesses a cell-like structure isomorphic to a disk, this work addresses a distinct scenario. Furthermore, this investigation reveals a significant geometric link: the Veech disk, a specific Teichmüller space utilized in dynamics and low-dimensional topology, is connected to the boundary of the aforementioned Hitchin link. The widespread adoption of scrum in software development has driven a surge in remote work through telecommuting. To address these issues, this study employs a multi-method approach to investigate the influence of telecommuting on the efficiency of agile projects. It utilizes project archives to assess changes in development metrics and conducts interviews to examine team members' perspectives on productivity shifts. Interviews further reveal that although teleworkers initially struggle with maintaining focus, they ultimately achieve a state of productivity comparable to pre-telecommuting levels. Furthermore, both the research methodology and results contribute to the broader understanding of remote work dynamics within the context of agile development.

This study examines elliptic flow ($v_2$) for B mesons and semi-leptonic B decays using both direct and indirect techniques within central Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 5.02 TeV. The analysis focuses on transverse momentum ranges of $0.2 < p_{\rm T} < 1$ GeV/$c$ for B mesons and $1 < p_{\rm T} < 10$ GeV/$c$ for decays via semi-leptonic channels. The findings reveal that the $p_{\text{t}}$-dependent $v_2$ for B mesons aligns with predictions from hydrodynamic models, whereas the $p_{\text{t}}$-dependent $v_2$ in B decays via semi-leptonic processes exceeds model predictions. This paper investigates the performance gap between optimal and binary power levels in multi-user interference networks. We demonstrate that for a $K$-user interference setup, the maximum loss in Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) incurred by using binary power instead of optimal power scales as $\Theta(\sqrt{K})}$. To achieve this result, we employ a novel analytical approach that bounds the difference as $\Theta(d^2)$, where $d^2$ represents the squared Euclidean distance from the point representing the current GDoF regime to the convex hull of previously identified optimal regimes. By leveraging this method, we can characterize the impact of power control across a broad spectrum of network configurations.

The expanding volume of electronic data in business settings has heightened the necessity for effective information auditing. This study introduces an innovative classification approach for auditing, grounded in adaptive patterns, that integrates the evidence theories of formal concept analysis and Dempster-Shafer calculations. By synthesizing these techniques, the methodology offers a nuanced perspective on attribute relationships and effectively manages uncertainty. The utility of this modeling strategy is validated through a formal audit of auditing practices, demonstrating its capacity to deliver a more granular and precise audit of information resources.

This work presents a method for sample generation based on the Strauss point process, a model that models limited point interactions. A core technique involves decomposing the Strauss point process into two independent Poisson point processes through stitching; these are then sampled separately before being merged. To achieve the sample generation, one must solve for the stitching exponent, a task that can be addressed via the Newton-Raphson method. The discussion covers two strategies: globally solving for the stitching exponent or approximating it locally. The latter approach partitions a specific region into smaller subareas, treating the Strauss interaction as negligible within each. By assuming Poisson distributions for the stitching exponent, one can then sample and merge. The effectiveness of these stitching approaches was assessed by contrasting their outputs with standard MCMC results.

The deformation of standard Lorentz and Galilean transformation rules, arising from the application of GUP, is examined. The discussion centers on the GUP framework, specifically the y-deformation associated with a dual GKP symmetry and its corresponding first-order speed modifications. We demonstrate that the symmetries of this first-order Lorentz and Galilean transformation remain identical for both space and momentum positions, regardless of the specific parameter values. Furthermore, we establish that a specific GKP first-speed model can be derived from a dual action principle, and we show that the dual Lorentz and Galilean transformations, along with time dilation and length contraction effects, align precisely with those predicted by GBG theory.

Our findings indicate that integrating multitasking into the model significantly improves the quality of generated timetables, while applying CP to refine an initial solution generated by ML proves to be a particularly effective strategy.

The Internet of Things (IoT) is rapidly expanding, with a particular emphasis on wireless mesh networks (WMNs) that leverage existing Wi-Fi infrastructure to facilitate large-scale deployments. These systems are currently reconfiguring smart homes and offices to enable real-time data exchange and automated decision-making. However, maintaining WMNs is challenging; once deployed, adding new nodes or upgrading existing ones often disrupts the network, and the impact of such changes on network performance remains insufficiently understood. This study addresses these gaps by investigating WMN resilience against failures and configuration updates through a controlled performance evaluation. Specifically, we assess the effectiveness of seamless firmware upgrades on a WMN of substantial size. Our findings indicate that these upgrades significantly reduce the impact of non-responsive (unresponsive) nodes and effectively counteract performance degradation caused by increasing network density.

Multifractal properties characterize eigenstates in non-interacting disordered systems that are in the thermalizing phase. Similar multifractality is anticipated for few-particle states beyond many-body localization (MBL) in disordered interacting systems, though the single-particle shift $\lambda_c^1$ and $N$-particle MBL transition $\lambda_c^N$ generally differ. By investigating the Fock-space EE dynamics, we have determined these crossover scales $\lambda_c^N$ for two-dimensional short-range models. Our findings indicate that $\lambda_c^N$ scales with system size $L$ as $1/L$ and converges toward the single-particle transition point $\lambda_c^1$ in large systems. Additionally, we observe that eigenstates near this transition exhibit multifractality.

This study examines the budget-constrained interactive search problem across $m$ hidden items, which are revealed one by one to the searcher. The process terminates when a selected budget of queries has been exhausted, a win is achieved by marking a chosen item as a win before the process ends, or a loss is incurred otherwise. The objective is to maximize the probability of a successful outcome. In the non-adversarial setting, the location of these items remains static throughout the search, whereas in the adversarial scenario, an adaptive adversary selectively hides items after each query. This paper establishes that the optimal strategy for the non-adversarial case is significantly simpler than previously thought, whereas the complexity of the optimal strategy for the adversarial case is comparable to that of the classic single-item, budget-constrained, static problem. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the optimal strategy for the non-adversarial scenario is a specific instance of the optimal strategy for the adversarial scenario. Finally, we present a novel algorithm that performs nearly as well as the optimal approach in the non-adversarial context but requires only a single round of queries per step.

Generative-adversarial networks have garnered significant interest for generating robust adversarial examples to test the robustness of deep learning models. While this approach is applicable to various tasks, including regression and classification, as well as time-series and image data, it has received minimal investigation within the context of quantum machine learning. This study introduces global adversarial examples for quantum classifiers, specifically Q-SVM and the quantum equivalent of a multi-layer perceptron (QMLP). These examples are created using a novel generator architecture based on quantum circuits. The objective function for training these instances is optimized using the global adversarial method, employing the classical stochastic gradient descent algorithm. The resulting global adversarial instances demonstrate superior robustness compared to locally derived variants. Additionally, the paper investigates the impact of various quantum disturbances on model performance and outlines strategies to mitigate them.

The research investigates the Steklov spectrum on domains in $\mathbb{R}^n$ whose boundaries nearly resemble an $n$-ball. By establishing an asymptotic expansion for Steklov eigenvalues as the approximation approaches a sphere, we identify the coefficients of the initial cubic term as specific functionals dependent on the corresponding Steklov eigenfunctions.

Compliance constitutes a core concept in compliance engineering, representing a predefined rule or constraint that governs how system execution traces should behave. Compliance checking involves determining whether a specific trace adheres to a given set of such constraints. This paper introduces a novel framework for verifying compliance within a new class of trace segments known as infix and postfix alignments. Unlike traditional models that rely on prefix alignments—where traces share common initial prefixes—these segment types allow shared suffixes or initial parts of varying lengths. Consequently, our approach enables the integration of compliance rules defined on different system architectures or protocol variants without requiring them to start from a common initial prefix. The proposed method provides a computationally efficient mechanism to validate whether a specific alignment satisfies a compliance constraint, regardless of whether the traces operate under a common underlying protocol.

Accurate modeling of signal propagation in cellular networks is fundamental for network planning, optimization, and the deployment of new technologies. Traditionally, this is achieved using empirical path-loss models, which offer limited accuracy in new environments due to their inability to account for all variables affecting signal attenuation. In contrast, machine learning models have demonstrated the ability to predict multi-story signal propagation with high accuracy. This study introduces a deep learning approach based on a 3D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) that utilizes a dataset of 3D point clouds. This architecture maps the raw point cloud data directly to multi-floor predictions, thereby eliminating the need for data alignment or the reconstruction of missing elements. We evaluate the model's performance against a baseline empirical method and a shallow learning CNN, demonstrating that the proposed approach yields significantly improved accuracy.

This objective was realized through a collaborative effort among researchers and industry experts, facilitated by a workshop that also served to gather critical feedback on the proposed definitions. We conclude by demonstrating how these established semantics can rigorously confirm validated checks for temporal planning problems, ensuring the correctness of the solutions derived.

This paper examines the global well-posedness of Vlasov-Poisson systems confined to bounded domains under Dirichlet boundary conditions. Specifically, we prove that both deterministic and random global solutions exist and are uniquely defined. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these solution statistics remain independent of the specific realizations of initial probability distributions in the stochastic setting. These findings are then applied to a class of Vlasov-Poisson-like models.

Although numerous methods exist for identifying visual concepts within images, they typically depend on user inputs like tags or lists of names. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach for automatic detection of visual concepts without any prior human annotations. A central element of this system is a new "Search Term Recognition" (STRICT) model, which predicts search queries in reverse: given a specific region within an image, the model generates the corresponding search phrase. A key innovation is that these phrases are automatically extracted by querying the same image using an inverse QBE query (Query By Image), eliminating the need for manual labels. By leveraging search metadata accumulated across millions of images, our approach demonstrates strong potential for tapping into extensive human search behaviors. Comprehensive experiments across various benchmarks validate that the proposed method surpasses existing baselines. Additionally, we demonstrate that incorporating these generated search terms as external knowledge enhances the performance of visual concept localization tasks.

Colloidal gels are vital in numerous applications, though their mechanical behavior and dynamics under fluid flow are critically dependent on both gel microstructure and external factors. In this study, we apply ultrasonic waves to colloidal gels to induce temporary, extreme modifications to their viscoelastic properties and demonstrate a new method for tailoring the rheological response of these materials. We conducted a systematic investigation of the rheo-acoustic behavior of both un- and gelated colloidal suspensions, revealing that the gel's mechanical stiffness can be stiffened or weakened depending on the applied acoustic frequency. Furthermore, we analyzed how these suspations respond to shear and ultrasonic energy during controlled shear rate sweeps, finding that the gelation process is accelerated by acoustic energy and that the resulting viscoelasticity mirrors that of the static (non-sonicated) gel. These findings offer a versatile strategy for manipulating the rheo-acoustic characteristics of diverse soft matter systems.

Math and science, along with the associated fields of STEM, are foundational to contemporary scientific and engineering disciplines. Nevertheless, the majority of existing research in document analysis and text mining focuses predominantly on natural language. Consequently, there is a growing need to develop specialized techniques for mathematical and STEM content. This study introduces a new approach to categorizing mathematical and STEM research papers, which leverages key features of text mining—specifically, entity recognition and extraction. We utilize the Cloud7 Math Entity Association (MESA) model, a method that maps the structural relationships among mathematical expressions within a single cloud, rather than relying on the traditional sparse matrices derived from bag-of-words representations. By integrating these expression structures with word embeddings, the approach generates comprehensive term-vectors that capture both semantic meaning and mathematical logic. Experimental results demonstrate that this method significantly enhances the accuracy of research paper categorization compared to conventional bag-of-words models.

In the context of a $2n$-person game where participants are paired up to compete in a secondary contest and only the winners receive a prize, players must decide whether to accept a pre-established pair or propose a new one. This paper introduces a model of "stable pairing" that clarifies how such pre-established matches are generated. Specifically, it posits that players are initially randomly offered proposals; however, if a player accepts a suggestion, the slot is removed from further offers, thereby influencing future proposal availability.

The analysis demonstrates that, given the set of proposal opportunities, players will choose partners to form a stable configuration. This outcome is driven by a unique off-equilibrium threat: if the game proceeds to the second game without a match, the random second stage is played, awarding prizes solely based on those random random pairings. Since the random nature of second-game pairings generally favors some potential players over others, players are motivated to avoid the random phase by securing a mutually agreed-upon pre-game arrangement.

The proposal mechanism described in this work is characterized by its efficiency, as it results in the allocation of second-game prizes to the correct set of winners. It is worth noting that this preference for stability is not universal; it depends entirely on the specific payoff structure of the second game. Generating abstractive summaries that are both coherent and coherent has long been a difficult and pivotal area within Natural Language Processing (NLP). Although automated evaluation metrics for machine summarization have seen significant recent advancements, they fail to achieve the same level of success as automated evaluation metrics for machine summarization that have been shown to be successful in other areas. This discrepancy suggests that current scoring methods do not fully capture summary quality. To address this, the authors propose SummScore, a new evaluation metric designed to better reflect the quality of abstractive summaries. SummScore is built on a pre-trained CrossEncoder model, utilizing a fine-tuned DeBERTa-v3 base model, and is trained on a diverse collection of high-quality reference summaries drawn from multiple datasets. This approach allows SummScore to effectively differentiate between excellent and mediocre summaries across various summarization tasks. Furthermore, the model excels at detecting specific types of errors in generated abstract text, such as hallucinations or irrelevance to the source. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SummScore outperforms existing state-of-the-art evaluation metrics on multiple datasets, achieving F1 scores that surpass the current best by 10% to 20%.

This scenario is highly relevant to experimental physics, particularly in reconstructing collision outcomes from particle trajectories or reconstructing images from lensless imaging data. We establish that our proposed technique restores the signal efficiently with high precision (up to a small failure risk) as long as a sufficient amount of data (up to a small number of errors) is available. Sensor fusion is a critical component of 3D object detection in autonomous driving systems. Although most current methods are confined by specific model constraints or lack generality, this study introduces BEVFusion, a novel and highly efficient LiDAR-camera fusion architecture. By leveraging a bird's-eye-view (BEV) feature map, BEVFusion delivers competitive performance across multiple backbones while offering superior model efficiency. Diverging from traditional strategies that rely on bounding box predictions, our approach utilizes feature-level fusion to enhance robustness against adverse weather and optical conditions. Additionally, we developed BEVFusion as a fundamental yet powerful fusion framework, demonstrating that its simplicity allows for extensive adaptation to diverse scenarios. Empirical evaluations on the nuScenes dataset confirm that our method achieves top-tier performance, even when integrated with lightweight network architectures.

This study investigates the impact of finite temperature on dissipation-range turbulence within Takaishi's model, which incorporates both thermal fluctuations and additive heat sources. The analysis demonstrates that the spectral energy distribution at the dissipation scale remains unaffected by the nature of the heat input, provided the system is in a steady state. This contrasts sharply with the inertial range, where pure thermal source models fail to account for the energy spectrum observed in simulations, whereas models incorporating both sources align well with simulation data. When examining the ratio of the dissipation-range to inertial-range spectra, a distinct dependence on temperature emerges, which is accurately captured by a theoretical framework derived from two-point correlation functions.

This research investigates the mechanisms driving complex diffraction patterns generated by laser-induced periodic surface structures (LIPSS) on liquids through rigorous simulations incorporating thermal diffusion and laser absorption. We establish that thermal gradients drive local surface instabilities, which in turn create a strong far-field scattering associated with these structures. Additionally, we demonstrate that the resulting spatially non-uniform temperature profile and varying curvature lead to distinct optical phenomena, including a flat-plate-like lensing effect and divergent beam characteristics. These findings offer a clear pathway to engineering specific optical functionalities by tailoring laser parameters to control liquid surface morphology.

Design dialogues involving human-computer interaction, whether mediated by software tools or human experts, are central to software development. However, extracting and reusing knowledge from these interactions remains difficult. To address this, we introduce a new methodology that automatically discovers natural language summaries of such dialogues, facilitating the retrieval of semantically similar instances. To ensure high retrieval accuracy, we introduce the Context Mining and Evaluation (CM&E) dataset, which contains 1,000 design dialogues. Evaluation against this corpus reveals that while state-of-the-art techniques struggle with direct application, our proposed approach achieves a Recall@5 score of 0.81. Robustness analysis further demonstrates that design dialogues possess distinct structural and semantic traits that differ from other text genres.

This study introduces H-STREAM, a novel large-analytic framework designed to support online queries over massive streams and their accumulated histories. Built upon the T-STREAM architecture—which utilizes the Tensor Tensor Store (STS) for efficient tensor operations—H-STREAM extends this foundation with a novel historical memory layer named HistTensorStore. This addition enables the efficient storage and retrieval of stream aggregates. The system is implemented in Python and provides a comprehensive, user-friendly API for constructing end-to-end analytics pipelines. Its capabilities include seamless integration with various data sources, connection to visualization tools, and direct access to both HistTensorStore and T-Store instances. To validate its practical application, the authors present a case study on climate analytics, where H-STREAM facilitates real-time inference for land-use classification. The system's query performance is benchmarked against the original T-STREAM version and the Hadoop data lake, with the latter serving as a reference point.

This work investigates non-resonant configurations in the single production of third-generation quark-antiquark pairs at hadron colliders. We analyze the kinematic structures arising from these events and introduce a new set of observables to characterize them. By evaluating these measures across various non-resonant scenarios, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this proposal. Specifically, we highlight the utility of our suggested observables for discriminating between different physics models in collider searches for third-generation partners.

The academic community increasingly relies on venue-specific metrics, such as acceptance and impact rates, to evaluate research outcomes. This approach, however, has been criticized for introducing biases based on decision-making quality and lack of transparency regarding impact measurements. To address these issues, we introduce a methodology that substitutes venue-specific metrics with entity-level metrics grounded in real citations. This study demonstrates that this citation-driven alternative effectively mitigates biases associated with traditional acceptance and impact rate metrics.

This paper investigates neural network (NN) control systems through a validation framework. Specifically, we propose characterizing such systems by delineating the state and input conditions that lead to instability or violation of constraints. To achieve this, we define two critical sets: the set of maximum divergence, representing the largest separation between the NN control output and that of any fixed comparator, and the set of constraint violation, which comprises operating conditions where the NN control results in breaches of system constraints. Utilizing Lyapunov methods, we characterize the set of largest negative Lyapunov derivative, which corresponds to the conditions yielding the steepest rate of Lyapunov function increase. By analyzing these three sets, we derive a method to quantify the sensitivity of NN control to perturbations in states and inputs, as well as to assess the likelihood of constraint violations under stochastic disturbances. Finally, we demonstrate the efficacy of this analysis using a validated network applied to a simple double integrator model.

This study introduces a hierarchical grouping method designed to accommodate overlapping structures and is derived through the optimization of extensional functors. We establish that the broadly applicable extensional functor for relational grouping—previously proven to guarantee optimally funtorial intensional grouping goals—is uniquely characterized by a "locality" property. Applying this locality property yields a specific extensional functor that solves the locality-based optimization problem, resulting in a hierarchical grouping algorithm. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness on both synthetic data and real-world datasets.

Restoring visual data from one-way compressed measurements is a critical challenge in practical applications, often involving high-dimensional tensor recovery from highly corrupted sources. This study introduces a new method for streaming tensor restoration that leverages patch-level monitoring. The core mechanism involves streaming through raw corrupted tensors and vectorizing small patches sequentially to reconstruct corresponding corresponding restored patches using a streaming Tensor Ring (TR) model. To ensure patch consistency, an adaptive constraint is applied during reconstruction, and a novel patch consistency loss is developed to enhance recovery quality. The approach is implemented using online Tikhonov regularization with a streaming TR model to restore each individual patch. The effectiveness of this method is validated on real-world video recovery tasks, including video surveillance and medical imaging. The results indicate that the method achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods on tensor recovery while demanding significantly less memory and computational resources.

This study employs direct numerical simulations to investigate three-dimensional turbulence within a rotating frame, focusing on the energy spectrum in wavenumbers satisfying $k_\perp \gg k_\parallel$. Leveraging recent theoretical frameworks, we demonstrate that the spectral distribution aligns with the predictions of the Zakharov-Kolmogorov (ZK) law, $E(k_\perp) \sim k_{\perp}^{-7/3}$, across a significant range of scales. The key driver of this Zakharov-Kolmogorov behavior is the $k_\parallel$ cascade, a phenomenon previously predicted by theory and now confirmed by our computational results.

This paper examines the relationship between the iterative graph standardization problem and the maximization of the smallest degree in the graph. It establishes that the two problems are equivalent if and only if the graph is either a complete graph or a complete multipartite graph. Furthermore, the text provides a characterization of the maximal-degree autonomous sets for arbitrary graphs and demonstrates the computational complexity of determining the smallest achievable maximum degree for the iterated standardization of an input graph, which is NP-hard.

The equilibrium equation governing the electrostatic potential within a graphene layer subjected to an external electric field is solved numerically, enabling the calculation of a new thermodynamic state variable: the graphene regulation factor. The study examines how this factor behaves in relation to the relative permittivity of the surrounding medium and the intensity of the applied electric field. The results indicate that the regulation factor remains constant under specific conditions and possesses a minimum value at others. The article further explores two operating modes of graphene acted upon by an external electrostatic field, detailing the corresponding mechanisms and their physical implications.

This research introduces AVATAR, a system designed to capture and render human skeletons in real-time alongside their faces and bodies. By utilizing ANIC, our method employs a machine learning model that translates skeletal movements into detailed images. Specifically, we trained our model using the "SKELETON" dataset, which includes motion capture data alongside synchronized video. To ensure precise video generation, our model incorporates a specialized loss function called Motion Capture Loss, optimizing the output based on the visual differences between predicted and actual video frames. Experimental results show that AVATAR successfully produces high-quality video outputs even when dealing with complex movements and varied lighting conditions.

The proliferation of image enhancement tools and software has drastically altered the landscape of digital imagery. While current research indicates that humans are generally able to detect such manipulations, their capability diminishes as alterations become more severe. This study proposes that a model, specifically trained on a variant of the Real/Fake detection task, exhibits the inverse behavior: human detection rates drop sharply as intensity rises, whereas model performance remains robust. This observation underscores the necessity for developing more effective methods capable of identifying aggressive alterations, thereby safeguarding individuals and systems from malicious digital content.

This paper explores topological link symbols and their emergence from Chern-Simons theory. It outlines how these symbols can be constructed using quasispin, provides a quasispin-based construction of them, and examines their connection to the Askey-Wilson algebra. Furthermore, it establishes relationships between these symbols and generalized Hahn polynomials, and it investigates multiple variable extensions of the generalized Hahn polynomials. These extended Hahn polynomials are shown to be eigenfunctions of a three-term recurrence relation, with the associated recurrence coefficients being explicitly constructed.

We examine the ground state properties of a 2D trimer antiferromagnet with inter-trimer coupling $J_H$ and intratrimer coupling $J_V$. Our findings indicate that the system undergoes a phase transition to a valence bond solid (VBS) state upon crossing the quantum critical point as $J_H$ decreases below the critical value $J^*$. Employing the Swendsen-Wege algorithm, we precisely locate this critical point for $J_H$ at $J^* = 0.240(1)J_V$ through finite-size scaling. Additionally, we computed the magnetization gap, dimer density, and long-range order parameter near the critical region to validate our results.

Although large pre-trained language models have proven effective for few- and zero-shot tasks, their performance often falls short of task-specific fine-tuned systems. This paper introduces a solution that simultaneously fine-tunes multiple NLP models using a unified objective to handle a diverse set of zero-shot tasks. By treating each task as structured with its own training data and a corresponding "cue" (such as answer classes or open-book references), the authors enable the simultaneous optimization of the systems across these different domains. The process involves gathering a collection of similar tasks, constructing a dataset of synthetic training examples for each, and formulating the relevant cues for that task's training. Experiments conducted across different NLP domains demonstrate that this joint fine-tuning strategy allows the initial systems to achieve performance on par with or superior to those adapted to individual single tasks.

The two Higgs boson masses observed at the LHC are accurately predicted by a two-Higgs-sector framework, offering a viable extension of the Standard Model. The extended Standard Model, known as the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (NMSM), is a particularly attractive candidate due to its elegant gauge hierarchy resolution, natural dark matter candidate, and capacity to accommodate the LHC Higgs data. This paper investigates the electroweak phase transition (EWPT) within the most general non-minimal supersymmetric standard model (NMSSM), which incorporates a $Z_3$ symmetry. This specific symmetry ensures the absence of a tree-level potential term involving three Higgs doublets, thereby facilitating a first-order phase transition. This transition is crucial for explaining the matter-antimatter asymmetry of the universe. Furthermore, we examine the implications of LHC measurements and dark matter constraints on first-order phase transitions, as well as the potential to detect gravitational waves.

We propose 'high-z Sudoku', a new observational strategy for submillimeter astronomy, designed to map the cosmic graphology surrounding distant galaxies. Our method involves strategically placing high-redshift targets within 'red zones'—areas of the sky devoid of foreground sources—to maximize the likelihood of discovering peer cosmological neighbors. By focusing on these pristine regions, we can significantly boost our discovery rates of distant galaxies. Our analysis of current High-Z Sudoku feasibility indicates that the approach is effective, with our simulated red zones yielding a 10% higher density of sub-mm luminous sources than the full sky average. Consequently, the technique promises a 20% to 30% improvement in observing efficiency for the APEX telescope. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the method remains robust even in crowded fields, provided the target source exhibits only minor (sub-100 milliarcsecond) positional shifts.

Our findings reveal that $O_\mathrm{max}(T)$ exhibits an upturn at a specific temperature, $T_\mathrm{max}$, which increases with system size; the impingement of this quantity on zero at very large scales serves as a marker for a symmetry-disordered phase at low temperatures. Additionally, we analyze the temperature dependence of the entanglement entropy, finding that its peak also shifts to higher temperatures as the system size grows. This study introduces a new kinetic model featuring a collision frequency that varies with molecular speed to more accurately simulate potential energy interactions in rarefied gas flows. The model's theoretical validity is demonstrated by deriving the equilibrium Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution analytically and establishing unique properties for both the weakly collisional (free molecular) and continuum regimes. In addition, rarefied flow scenarios around a sphere and flat plate are analyzed using an iterative scheme that couples the kinetic model with boundary conditions. The resulting predictions for dimensionless drag and skin friction coefficients are compared against those from the Bird model and continuum-based simulations, respectively. Comparative analysis reveals that the new kinetic model yields significantly closer alignment with results from continuum simulations than Bird's approach.

We propose a novel approach for developing task-specific semantic models that begin by pre-training on extensive, domain-agnostic corpora. This is followed by adaptation to a target domain through the use of extensive or limited extensive corpora, and, in the most data-constrained scenarios, the system is further refined using a very small set of meticulously crafted and manually annotated training data. We demonstrate that this strategy allows for the efficient scaling of models with specific task-related knowledge, even when operating under extreme data limitations. Our analysis reveals that the proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques in few-shot settings, specifically for applications such as machine reading comprehension and question answering. Additionally, we evaluate the model's adaptability across diverse tasks and domains, examining the impact of the initial stage of training on its performance.

The future Electron-Iron Collider (EIC) is planned to operate electron-proton and electron-nucleus collisions with a center-of-mass energy between 200 and 350 GeV. To accurately reconstruct the scattered electron and the scattered proton or nucleus, the EIC detector requires advanced silicon tracking sensors. This review examines the current advancements in these silicon sensors and outlines a strategy for scaling sensor production to meet EIC requirements. Additionally, the study presents a roadmap for theEIC silicon tracker, detailing critical design parameters and a production schedule. A full-size prototype has been fabricated and tested under the stringent radiation environment of the future EIC detector. Results from this testing demonstrate that the sensor fulfills all performance specifications for this application.

The variability observed in the near-infrared (NIR) and X-ray bands of low-mass active solar-type stars is often attributed to magnetic activity, but this explanation is less clear for supermassive black holes, or active galactic nuclei (AGNs). While the standard model for active solar-type stars involves a combination of magnetic and mass ejections, it is uncertain whether similar phenomena occur in AGNs, given that their accreting black holes are generally considered to lack strong magnetic fields. Instead, AGN variability is frequently interpreted as the response of the black hole-accretion disk system to magnetic or mass ejections. This study investigates the nature of outbursts in the NIR and X-ray emissions of low-mass AGNs, specifically targeting the nearby low-luminosity active galactic nucleus NGC 4395. Analysis of the X-ray outburst in NGC 4395 reveals a damped oscillation with a period of approximately 1.5 days, while the simultaneous infrared outburst displays a complex, non-oscillatory light curve. These findings suggest that the outbursts in NGC 4395 are unlikely to be oscillations, but rather the result of a mass ejection event.
